families.name: The Big Book and other core texts

themes.name: Charter protection for the Big Book
themes.scope: Amend the Conference Charter (Article 3, or Article 12 / Appendix L) so that changes to the first 164 pages, The Doctor's Opinion, Dr. Bob's Nightmare, Forewords etc. need the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups (the protection the Steps and Traditions have), or a similar formal lock.
themes.lede: Thirty-two proposals ask the Conference to give the Big Book's core text the same formal protection that the Twelve Steps, the Twelve Traditions and the Charter's Article 12 Warranties already have: no change without the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups. They differ on which pages are covered, which edition is meant and where the wording would go.

background.text: The original Conference Charter, adopted in 1955, said no change in A.A. Tradition could be made without the written consent of two-thirds of all A.A. groups. That article did not mention the Big Book.
background.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 120 (Original Conference Charter, Article 3); M-39 p. 144

background.text: The 1955 Resolution that made the Conference the successor to the co-founders says the Traditions and the Article 12 Warranties may be changed only after the groups are notified and given at least six months, and only with the written consent of at least three-quarters of the registered groups that respond.

In 1957, at Bill W.'s suggestion, the Conference amended Article 3 so that changes to Article 12, the Traditions or the Steps need the written consent of three-quarters of the groups. In 1969 the wording was updated to name 'the Twelve Traditions of A.A.'

In 1976 the Conference resolved that the Twelve Steps are among the texts that need three-quarters of responding groups to change, and had a bracketed note added saying 'registered groups' includes all groups known to general service offices around the world.

The Charter does not name the Big Book. Its core text is covered instead by an Advisory Action: in 1995 the Conference recommended that the first 164 pages, the Preface, the Forewords, 'The Doctor's Opinion,' 'Doctor Bob's Nightmare' and the Appendices 'remain as is.'

In 2024 the trustees' Literature Committee took no action on a proposal to write into the Charter that these sections would never change, noting that this was not a widely expressed need of the Fellowship.

In 2025 four proposals to expand Article Three to protect the co-founders' writings went to the Conference Committee on Report and Charter. It took no action, noting that the definition of 'co-founders' writings' needed further clarification before any change in policy or in the Charter.

The 2025 Conference also asked the General Service Board to classify A.A. World Services and Grapevine literature written before 1971 as Recovery, Service or Archival/Historical. Reviewing the progress report in 2026, the Report and Charter committee noted there is no formal definition of 'founders' and asked that the topic go to the trustees' Literature Committee for further input. The 2026 proposal grid (110 items) had no Article 3 amendment; this year's has 32.
background.cite: M-39 p. 163; 2026 Final Report pp. 51-52; proposal grid for the 76th Conference (2026)

themes.now: Charter Article 3 says no change in Article 12 or in the Twelve Traditions or Twelve Steps may be made with less than the written consent of three-quarters of the A.A. groups, as the 1955 Resolution describes. The Big Book is not named. Two submitters cite page 123; in the 2026-2028 Service Manual the current text is on page 124.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 124 (Current Conference Charter, Article 3)
themes.asked: Thirty-two items (grid pages 10-18, trustees' General Service Conference Committee). 24 name Article 3 or rewrite its three-quarters sentence; others name Article 12 (#201), Appendix L (#10), 'Article 4' (#189) or no article. All cover the first 164 pages; 31 add The Doctor's Opinion, 23 Dr. Bob's story, 10 Prefaces or Forewords, 3 the book Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions. Nine are identical (#72, #95, #119, #120, #136-#139, #143).
raised: Several submitters say the goal is to give the Big Book's recovery text the same protection the Steps, Traditions and Warranties already have (for example #10, #62, #76, #201).
Some describe these pages as the founders' writings, the co-founders' text or the foundational text of A.A. (#23, #158, #76).

#158 would still allow mechanical corrections and new material outside the protected text, and #201 typographical, printing and formatting corrections; two others would require group consent even for grammar or spelling changes (#114, #115).
Two specify consent from registered groups worldwide (#14, #130).

considerations.text: How it would be decided: Bill W.'s Concept XII essay says the Charter's first eleven Articles can be readily amended by the Conference itself, while changing the Article 12 Warranties needs the written consent of three-quarters of the directory-listed groups that vote, with six months to deliberate. The Conference has amended Article 3 by its own action before (1957, 1969), and Articles 4 and 1 in 2020 and 2021. A proposal that amends Article 12 itself (#201) would fall under the group-consent rule.

How consent is counted: under the 1955 Resolution it is three-quarters of the registered groups that respond, after at least six months. A 1976 bracketed note extends 'registered groups' to all groups known to general service offices worldwide, a 2018 note says groups are listed only for accurate communication, and the Article 3 rule carries a note that it applies to the original English version only.

Reasons the committees gave: in 2025 Policy/Admissions said a policy on voting requirements might be premature before co-founders' writings are defined, and Report and Charter said that definition needed clarifying before changes in policy or the Charter; in 2026 Report and Charter noted there is no formal definition of 'founders.'
considerations.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 47-48, 51; 2026 Final Report p. 52

considerations.text: Which text: five proposals name the Fourth Edition and one the Fifth. The texts would differ, for example, in Chapter 7, where the 2026 Conference voted to replace the word 'Eskimo,' and in 'Bill's Story,' where the Publishing Department agreed to correct 'Plattsburg' to 'Plattsburgh' for the Fifth Edition, which also has a new preface and foreword.
considerations.cite: Proposal grid for the 77th Conference (Oct. 1, 2026); M-39 p. 106 (p3139); 2026 Final Report pp. 5, 101

questions: How is the Big Book's protection under the 1995 Advisory Action different from the protection the Charter gives the Steps and Traditions?
If the Big Book were added to Article 3, which parts and which edition should be named, and why?
How would written consent from three-quarters of responding groups be gathered and counted in practice, and which groups would be asked?
Should spelling or typographical corrections be treated the same way as changes of wording?
Should 'founders' writings' be defined before any Charter change, as the 2025 committees suggested?
themes.watch: The trustees' General Service Conference Committee decides at the Oct. 30-Nov. 2, 2026 board weekend which proposals go forward; the preliminary agenda follows in November. Watch which Conference committee receives these items and whether they are combined.

themes.name: Keep the Big Book text as it is (notes instead of changes)
themes.scope: Leave the first 164 pages (and other parts) unchanged; keep an unchanging 'original' edition; address history and culture with forewords, footnotes, a note to the reader or annotations instead of edits.
themes.lede: Eleven proposals favor keeping the Big Book's core wording unchanged, or adding context beside it instead of editing it. Four say the first 164 pages should not change; two would keep a fixed 'original' while updates go into a separate book; five would address history, culture or language with notes, prefaces, footnotes, an addendum or annotations.

background.text: When the Second Edition appeared in 1955, Bill W. told the Conference that 'not an iota' of the recovery text had been changed; the story section was changed and enlarged, and a new foreword was added beside the old one.

In 1976 delegates were asked to tell their areas that the Third Edition text was not being changed and only the stories were updated; in 1978 the Conference asked that the Second Edition foreword be printed as originally published.

In 1986 the Conference found no further explanation of out-of-date phrases or gender-oriented pronouns necessary, because the preface states the text was written in 1939 and has not been changed. A 1992 action found the 1986 actions adequate.

In 1993 a request to rewrite the first three chapters was not carried out because of strong sentiment against changing the first 164 pages. In 1995 the Conference recommended that those pages, the Preface, the Forewords, 'The Doctor's Opinion,' 'Doctor Bob's Nightmare' and the Appendices 'remain as is.'

For Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions the Conference chose an explanatory note: in 2002 it kept Bill W.'s text as originally published, and in 2005 it added an Introduction explaining the book's 1953 origin and why its language is kept.

Earlier Conferences (1977, reaffirmed 1993) decided against a facsimile of the first edition; in 2013 the Conference approved a commemorative 75th Anniversary Edition of the first edition, first printing, to be published in April 2014.

The 2021 decision to develop a Fifth Edition quoted the 1995 action and said the draft would include a new foreword, an updated preface and updates expanding on ideas in Appendices III and V. In 2026 the Conference approved the Fifth Edition with minor editorial changes and voted to replace 'Eskimo' in Chapter 7.

Similar requests came up before: the trustees' Literature Committee took no action in 2023 and 2024 on requests that these sections stay as they appear in the Fourth Edition, and in 2026 it sent a proposal for an acknowledging passage in the Fifth Edition foreword and footnotes to the Fifth Edition subcommittee.
background.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 89; 2024 Final Report p. 97; 2026 Final Report p. 104

themes.now: The 1995 Advisory Action, quoted again in 2021, says the first 164 pages, Preface, Forewords, 'The Doctor's Opinion,' 'Doctor Bob's Nightmare' and Appendices remain as is. The Fifth Edition approved in 2026 has 26 new stories, a new preface and foreword and updated appendices, and replaces one word in Chapter 7; books are expected in early February 2027.
themes.now_cite: M-39 pp. 94, 104, 106 (p2773, p3069, p3138, p3139); 2026 Final Report p. 5; app calendar (General Service Board Quarterly Report, 3rd quarter 2026 p. 7)
themes.asked: Eleven items. Four: the first 164 pages should not change (#30, #34, #118, #204). Two keep an unchanging 'original' with updates elsewhere: separate revised versions (#4, Big Book and Twelve and Twelve) or the Plain Language Big Book (#92). One keeps the Fourth Edition text, with notes for concerns (#199). Four want notes: a note to the reader (#26), a historical-context addendum (#52), a page 17 footnote (#94), annotations (#106).
raised: Submitters point to the book's 1939 origin: one would have a note invite readers to look for the meaning rather than at words that may offend (#26).

#106 says annotations on the historical and social context of the time would aid understanding and identification without changing the wording; #94 would add historical and present-day context on A.A.'s origins and growth into a worldwide Fellowship.
Two say a fixed original would let any modern-language revision happen in a separate book, whether new 'revised' versions (#4) or the Plain Language Big Book (#92).
One would handle historical or cultural concerns with added notes, prefaces or footnotes, leaving the text itself unaltered (#199).

considerations.text: The note approach has been used before: a 2005 Introduction to Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions explains why its language is kept, and a 2017 footnote to the pamphlet 'Problems Other Than Alcohol' says some of its 1958 language may be dated. In 1986, by contrast, the Conference found no added explanation needed for the Big Book because its preface already says the text was written in 1939 and has not been changed.

'Remain as is' has existed alongside specific Conference-approved edits in the listed sections: a sentence removed from the Fourth Edition Foreword (2002), punctuation in 'Dr. Bob's Nightmare' restored (2004), 'largely' restored to the Preface (2006), a Preface sentence corrected (2014) and a word replaced in Chapter 7 (2026). The Preface itself says the recovery text was left 'largely untouched.'

In 2023 a Conference committee listed this choice among questions for the trustees' Literature Committee to put to the Fellowship: should future changes keep the original writing with footnotes, or should founders' writings remain unchanged? The 2024 sharing that followed ran along three lines: no changes at all, changes reflecting current values and language, and slow change with broad input first.
considerations.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 42; 2024 Final Report p. 5

considerations.text: The 1995 'remain as is' statement is an Advisory Action of the Conference; the Charter proposals in this cycle would place a protection for much the same sections in the Charter itself, with a group-consent requirement.
considerations.cite: M-39 p. 94; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 124; proposal grid for the 77th Conference (Oct. 1, 2026)

questions: What does 'remain as is' mean to your group: no change to any word, or no change to the meaning?
What are the strengths and limits of explanatory notes, compared with editing the text?
Should there be an unchanging 'original' edition alongside a current one, and how would readers tell them apart?
If updates went only into the Plain Language Big Book, as #92 proposes, how would the role of each book change?
Which edition, the Fourth or the Fifth, should be the reference text for any preservation rule?
themes.watch: Fifth Edition books are expected in early February 2027. Watch whether the trustees' Literature Committee forwards the note and annotation proposals, and how the Conference treats them alongside the Charter and Fellowship-review items.

themes.name: Fellowship review before any Big Book change
themes.scope: Any proposed change to the Big Book (or Twelve and Twelve) must first go to the groups/areas through the proposed-agenda-item process, with background, waiting periods (often two years) or a higher Conference vote (two-thirds / three-quarters of voters) before final action.
themes.lede: Twenty-five proposals ask for Fellowship review before the Conference changes the Big Book's text, and in some cases Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions: sending changes through the proposed agenda item process or to the groups first, with background and time for a group conscience, waiting one or two years, or setting a Conference vote threshold.

background.text: In 1953 the Conference adopted, and in 1954 continued, a rule that no policy be declared or action taken on matters liable to gravely affect A.A. as a whole without the consent of at least three-quarters of the members present.
In 1978 the Conference recommended that delegates be made aware of any changes under consideration in the book Alcoholics Anonymous before publication.

In 2014 the Conference returned to the A.A. World Services (AAWS) board a proposed clarification of the AAWS publication policy. As quoted, the policy lets AAWS make needed editorial changes, but none to the Big Book's Preface, Forewords, 'The Doctor's Opinion,' first 164 pages, 'Dr. Bob's Nightmare' or Appendices without prior Conference approval; the clarification would have limited editorial changes to factual, statistical, capitalization, punctuation and spelling fixes. In 2020 the Conference accepted the AAWS board's January 2020 policy on updating pamphlets and other materials.

In 2023 the Conference Committee on Finance, which had the item under a workload-sharing plan, suggested that the trustees' Literature Committee seek Fellowship input on any future changes to the founders' literature, listing questions such as a two-year Conference review process and a threshold for review at group, district or area level.

Before the 2024 Conference, Conference members met online to share that input. It ran along three lines: no changes at all; changes based on current values, expressed need and more modern language; and changes made slowly, with broad Fellowship input first. The 2024 Finance committee then concluded that current procedures let each Conference consider proposals, 'negating the need for a mandated policy.'

A 2024 floor action asked for a 75% Conference vote, area discussions and a decision at a later Conference before changes to founders' writings take effect; it was among the floor actions recommitted to trustees' committees or boards.

In 2025 the Policy/Admissions committee took no action on a request for a supermajority to change founders' literature, saying a voting policy might be premature before co-founders' writings are defined, and noting that a two-year process might be considered. The trustees' General Service Conference Committee's follow-up grid then routed that topic to the chair of the trustees' Literature Committee.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 47-48, 90; 2026 Final Report p. 83

background.text: In 2026 the Chapter 7 word change came to the Conference as a Literature committee recommendation and a matching change in Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions as a floor action. A floor motion to suspend printing of the Fifth Edition until there was more consensus on procedures for founders' writings was declined.

themes.now: Apart from the 1995 'remain as is' action and a 1978 request that delegates hear of proposed changes before publication, a Big Book change is decided like any Advisory Action: substantial unanimity (a two-thirds vote), on a committee recommendation or a floor action. Article 3 leaves delegates free to decide which questions to take to the group level.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 42-43, 124; M-39 pp. 87, 94 (p2513, p2773); 2024 Final Report p. 43
themes.asked: Twenty-five items (grid pages 14-25, trustees' General Service Conference Committee). Eighteen ask that changes go through the proposed agenda item process, reach groups or areas, or wait for a later Conference; six would add this to Charter Article 3 (#82, #101, #132, #152, #168, #170). Three set a two-year review or wait (#86, #99, #167). Four set a vote: two-thirds (#87, #91, #209) or three-quarters (#93).
raised: Several submitters want groups to have background and time to form an informed group conscience, and delegates to hear from their areas, before any vote (#88, #123, #160, #202, #211).
One group says the change 'was not even on the agenda' and was not raised at district level (#148); another frames its request around transparency, trust and the 'upside-down triangle' (#45).

#187 asks that the exact current and proposed wording appear in background material, and says updates to language described as outdated or non-inclusive count as text changes rather than editorial ones; it presents itself as reaffirming the 1995 action.
Those asking for two years of review say it would allow broad participation (#86, #167).

considerations.text: Votes: Advisory Actions already need a two-thirds vote, so #87, #91 and #209 pair that threshold with Fellowship-wide consideration first; a recommendation that wins a simple majority but falls short of two-thirds is recorded in the Final Report but not sent to the board. The three-quarters vote in #93 resembles a rule the 1953 Conference adopted and the 1954 Conference continued for matters liable to gravely affect A.A. as a whole.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 42-43; M-39 p. 107 (p3157, p3167); proposal grid for the 77th Conference (Oct. 1, 2026)

considerations.text: How it would be decided: a Conference policy would be an ordinary Advisory Action, and a new paragraph in Article 3 falls within the first eleven Articles, which the Concept XII essay says the Conference can readily amend itself; only Article 12, the Steps and the Traditions need group consent.

Timing: proposals received by September 30 go to the trustees' committees, which decide at the fall board weekend which reach the Conference; background material on agenda items has reached Conference members in mid-February (Feb. 17-20 in 2026), about eight weeks before the April Conference.
considerations.cite: App calendar data (aa.org proposed agenda item page; 2025 Final Report p. 86; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 45; 2026 Final Report p. 84)

considerations.text: Editorial authority: #187 asks that no A.A. World Services publication policy, or editorial authority under it, be read to allow wording changes to these texts. The policy as quoted in 2014 already required prior Conference approval for editorial changes to these Big Book sections; a 2014 proposal to limit editorial changes to factual, statistical, capitalization, punctuation and spelling fixes was returned to the AAWS board, and in 2020 the Conference accepted the board's January 2020 policy on updating pamphlets and other materials.

questions: What should count as a change to the Big Book: any word, or only a change of meaning? Should spelling or typographical corrections be exempt?
How much time do the groups in your district need to study a proposed change and give their delegate an informed group conscience?
Should the Conference be able to act on a Big Book change that first comes up during Conference week, or should such a change always wait a year?
Which safeguard, if any, does your group prefer: a higher Conference vote, a waiting period, wider group discussion, or a mix?
How do these proposals fit with Article 3's statement that delegates decide which questions to take to the group level?
themes.watch: Watch whether the trustees forward these items this fall, to which committee (similar 2025 items went to Policy/Admissions), and whether the trustees' Literature Committee chair reports on the two-year-process and supermajority topic before the April 2027 Conference.

themes.name: Undo the 2026 “Eskimo” change
themes.scope: Rescind or reverse the 2026 Conference action that replaced the word “Eskimo” in the Big Book (Chapter 7, Working With Others), or the floor action behind it, and restore the word.
themes.lede: At its April 26 to May 2, 2026 meeting, the 76th Conference took two actions replacing “Eskimo” with “a neutral, non-racial term”: one in the Big Book chapter “Working With Others,” one in the Tradition Eight essay of Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions. Ten proposals for 2027 ask to undo a change; nine name the Big Book change.

background.text: The 1995 Conference recommended that the Big Book’s first 164 pages, Preface, Forewords, “The Doctor’s Opinion,” “Doctor Bob’s Nightmare” and Appendices “remain as is.”
In 2021 the Conference approved developing a Fifth Edition of the Big Book with updated stories, “keeping in mind” that 1995 action.
background.cite: 2021 Final Report p. 60; advisory action p3069

background.text: In 2022 a floor action to reaffirm the 1995 action appears in the Final Report’s list of floor actions that did not become Advisory Actions.

In March 2022 the words “Indian and Eskimo” were removed from the February 19 page of Daily Reflections under the A.A. World Services (AAWS) policy “Keeping A.A. Literature Current.” The trustees’ Literature Committee noted this in 2025 when a proposal asked for that change.

At the 2026 Conference the Conference Committee on Literature recommended, and the full Conference approved as an Advisory Action, that “Eskimo” be removed from Chapter 7, “Working With Others,” and replaced with a neutral, non-racial term. The same committee report carried the approval of the Fifth Edition with minor editorial changes.
background.cite: 2026 Final Report p. 40; advisory actions p3139, p3138 (M-39 p. 106)

background.text: A separate floor action (a motion made directly in the general session, not a committee recommendation) removed the word from the Twelve and Twelve essay on Tradition Eight, with the same neutral-term wording. The Final Report does not number its floor actions, and this is the only floor action about the word that it lists.
background.cite: 2026 Final Report p. 39; advisory action p3135 (M-39 p. 105)

background.text: The Literature committee, noting the Chapter 7 recommendation “if approved by the Conference,” suggested considering similar changes to the Spanish and French Big Books and other translations.

The report’s summary of the week says the Conference voted to remove “an offensive term from the first 164 pages,” which led to more discussion of founders’ writings. A floor action to suspend printing of the Fifth Edition until there was more consensus on procedures for changing “Founders’ Writings” was declined (the Conference voted not to consider it).

themes.now: Two 2026 Advisory Actions stand, accepted by the General Service Board after the Conference: the Big Book change (a Literature committee recommendation) and the Twelve and Twelve change (a floor action). Both say only “a neutral, non-racial term”; the Final Report names no replacement word and prints no vote counts. An Advisory Action needs at least a two-thirds vote.
themes.now_cite: 2026 Final Report pp. 39-40; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 53; advisory actions p3135, p3139
themes.asked: Ten proposals, all to the trustees’ Literature Committee. Nine ask to reverse the 2026 Big Book change and keep or restore the word (28, 33, 90, 124, 146, 159, 193, 203, 218; 159 and 203 are identical). One (89) asks to rescind “Floor Action #6 of the 76th Conference.” Five (89, 90, 124, 159, 203) want such changes to reach groups first. Item 69 also says to keep the word.
raised: Several submitters (89, 90, 124, 159, 203) say a change like this should first go through the regular agenda, with time for groups to form an informed group conscience before the Conference makes a final decision; 124 also asks for safeguards on future changes to the first 164 pages.
One group (146) cites the Fellowship’s wish to preserve founders’ writings and A.A. history.

Two districts in Area 78 (193) ask to rescind the Chapter 7 action as worded; a group and a district in Area 80 (218) ask to return to the 1995 Advisory Action, which they say has preserved the Big Book since Bill W.’s death.

One submitter (69) says words written in 1939 should not be read with present-day meanings; another group (148, in the review theme) says a recent Big Book change was not on the agenda or discussed at district level.

considerations.text: The Conference’s own wording gives its reason: both actions call for “a neutral, non-racial term,” and the report’s summary calls the word “an offensive term.”

On the agenda question: the Service Manual says delegates may bring items that did not leave committee, or were never on the agenda, as floor actions; the full Conference first votes on whether to consider one. The trustees’ Literature Committee’s report on what it did and did not send to the 2026 Conference (including the Fifth Edition draft and three Living Sober chapters) does not mention this word. A separate 2026 recommendation, referred to the General Service Board, asked the Conference to acknowledge that its committees may take up items not placed on their agenda.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 60; 2026 Final Report pp. 42, 100-107

considerations.text: On vote counts: the Final Report does not print tallies. At a 2026 Conference workshop, many participants said they value not reporting vote tallies, since actions pass by substantial unanimity.

How a reversal would be decided: after General Service Office staff review, a proposal goes to the trustees’ committee, which decides whether to forward it to a Conference committee. A recommendation becomes an Advisory Action only with substantial unanimity (two-thirds). The Big Book and Twelve and Twelve changes are separate actions, and the translations were raised separately.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 53-54, 182 (Appendix U); 2026 Final Report p. 48

questions: What difference, if any, does it make to your group that one change came from a committee recommendation and the other from a floor action?
How does your group read the 1995 “remain as is” action in relation to a one-word change?
If the Big Book wording were restored, should the Twelve and Twelve and the translations follow the same decision?
What background would your group want before forming a group conscience on this request?
When vote counts are not printed, how can members learn how a Conference reached a decision?
themes.watch: At the Oct 30 to Nov 2, 2026 board weekend the trustees’ Literature Committee decides whether these go to the 77th Conference (April 11-17, 2027). Watch the November preliminary agenda and any grouping with review proposals.

themes.name: Define and protect “founders’ writings”
themes.scope: Define which texts are co-founders' / founders' writings (Big Book parts, Twelve and Twelve, Language of the Heart, As Bill Sees It, A.A. Comes of Age, letters, pre-1971/72 publications ...), set a policy or moratorium on changing them, an editorial policy, or a 'historically significant literature' class.
themes.lede: “Founders’ writings” is used often but has never been formally defined by the Conference. These proposals ask the Conference to say which texts count, and to set rules before any more of them are changed. Suggested rules include a pause on changes, an editorial policy, or a special class of historic literature.

background.text: Under the 1955 Resolution the Conference became the “sole successors” of the co-founders, and Charter Article 4 says it replaces the founders as guides to the board. Since a 1957 amendment suggested by Bill W., Article 3 has required the written consent of three-quarters of the groups to change Article 12, the Traditions or the Steps; in 1976 the Conference confirmed that the Steps are among the documents needing that consent.
background.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 134-135, 139; advisory actions p4285, p4358 (M-39 pp. 144, 146)

background.text: Earlier Conferences singled out Bill W.’s writings: they were exempt from gender-neutral editing (1986), and his Twelve and Twelve text was to remain as originally published (2002).

In 2023 the Conference Committee on Finance, which had the item under a workload-sharing plan, suggested that the trustees’ Literature Committee seek Fellowship input on future changes to literature written by A.A.’s founders. Its suggested questions included a two-year review, footnotes versus no changes, a review threshold, whether the 2021 Twelve and Twelve changes should stay, and a policy on Bill W.’s writing.

By January 2024, 1,171 responses had come in, about two-thirds from individual members. The input shared before the 2024 Conference fell along three lines: make no changes; make changes reflecting current values and language; or change slowly, with broad Fellowship input first.

The 2024 Conference Committee on Finance took no action, saying current procedures let each Conference weigh proposals without a mandated policy. A 2024 floor action calling for a 75% vote and a later review at the second following Conference for changes to founders’ writings was among floor actions sent on to trustees’ committees.

In 2025 the Policy/Admissions committee took no action on a request for a higher vote to change founders’ literature, and Report and Charter took no action on revising Article Three. Both pointed to the need to define the term first. The Conference asked the board to classify all A.A. World Services (AAWS) and AA Grapevine literature written before 1971 as Recovery, Service or Archival/Historical.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 40, 47-48, 51, 89-90; advisory action p4819

background.text: In the 2025-26 cycle, three proposals asking to define founders or founders’ writings went to the General Service Board and were not forwarded to the Conference.
background.cite: 76th Conference proposed agenda item grid, items 17, 94, 97

background.text: In 2026 Report and Charter reviewed the classification progress report, noted “no formal definition of ‘founders’” and asked that the topic go to the trustees’ Literature Committee. The trustees’ General Service Conference Committee sent the 2025 ideas on a two-year process or a higher vote to the trustees’ Literature chair.

themes.now: No formal definition has been adopted. In 2026 the Conference’s Report and Charter committee noted that “founders” has no formal definition and asked that the classification topic go to the trustees’ Literature Committee. Only Article 12, the Traditions and the Steps need three-quarters of the groups to change; other literature changes are Advisory Actions needing two-thirds of the Conference.
themes.now_cite: 2026 Final Report p. 52; Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 53, 135
themes.asked: Thirteen (eight to the trustees’ General Service Conference Committee, five to Literature). Five ask for no changes, even spelling, to listed founders’ works until the Fellowship decides (42, 53, 107, 108, 111). Others: define and protect the term (122, 161); count every pre-1972 A.A. World Services or Grapevine publication (219); a protected class (164); a historical addendum (52); an editorial policy (173, 174); a voice from outside U.S./Canada (102).
raised: Two submitters (122, 161) say the Conference should define founders’ writings and set a policy before approving any further changes, with background and time for the whole Fellowship to take part.

Two districts in Area 78 (219) say their pre-1972 definition answers the 2025 Policy/Admissions response to six 2025 proposals, and ask that those proposals be brought back as a 2027 item to expand Charter Article Three.
Supporters of a pause (42, 53, 107, 108, 111, 173) want no changes until the Fellowship, or an editorial policy, decides how these texts may be changed.
Others propose that changes need substantial unanimity at two Conferences in a row (164), or that members outside the U.S./Canada structure have a way to take part (102).

considerations.text: The 2025 Policy/Admissions committee said setting voting rules may be premature before defining co-founders’ writings, and that a two-year process might be considered before any vote.

The 2026 Report and Charter committee noted that sorting literature into Recovery, Service or Historical could confuse, since content overlaps. It noted that “cofounders of A.A.” usually means Bill W. and Dr. Bob, though many people played founding roles in various places.

On a pause: in 2025 the trustees’ Literature Committee took no action on a proposed 2-3 year moratorium on non-editorial revisions and new A.A. World Services literature; it recognized the problem but said this would be seen as binding instruction upon future Conferences. It also took no action on a request for no changes to founders’ writings, noting that developing a group conscience through the service structure would help such proposals.

The three-quarters group-consent rule sits in Charter Article 3 and covers Article 12, the Traditions and the Steps. The 1955 Resolution describes how it works: groups are notified and given at least six months to respond.

questions: Which texts would your group count as founders’ writings: only Bill W.’s and Dr. Bob’s own words, everything published before 1971 or 1972, or something in between?
What kind of protection fits best: a waiting period, a higher Conference vote, a Charter change, or notes alongside the text?
Can one Conference bind later Conferences with a moratorium, and should it?
How should members outside the U.S./Canada structure be heard on books used around the world?
What would your group want to know about the board’s literature classification work before taking a position?
themes.watch: At the Oct 30 to Nov 2, 2026 board weekend, what the trustees’ General Service Conference and Literature committees do with these, whether they are grouped with Charter and review proposals, and any report on defining founders’ literature.

themes.name: Change or restore specific wording
themes.scope: A specific edit to the Big Book or Twelve and Twelve text: a word, sentence, pronoun, gendered or dated language, a story, an appendix, page numbering, or undoing an earlier specific edit (for example the 2021 Twelve and Twelve revisions).
themes.lede: These proposals ask for one specific edit to the Big Book or to Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions (the “Twelve and Twelve”). Some would remove dated or gendered words, some would restore earlier text, and some would add a story, a footnote or an appendix. The Conference has handled requests like these many times since the 1980s.

background.text: In 1984 the Conference declined to change a term for gay people on page 140 of the Twelve and Twelve, keeping Bill W.’s writings as first published.

In 1986 the Conference said that because the Big Book’s preface states the 1939 text is unchanged, no explanation of out-of-date phrases or gendered pronouns was needed. It asked editors to keep making other A.A. literature gender-neutral at reprint, except Bill W.’s writings. The 1992 Conference found these actions covered the issue.
background.cite: Advisory actions p2607, p2611, p2715 (M-39 pp. 89-93)

background.text: In 1995 the Big Book’s first 164 pages, Preface, Forewords, “The Doctor’s Opinion,” “Doctor Bob’s Nightmare” and Appendices were to “remain as is.” In 2002 the Conference kept Bill W.’s Twelve and Twelve text as originally published (a decision later described as unanimous). The same year it removed a sentence about electronic meetings from the Fourth Edition Foreword, and in 2005 it added an Introduction to the Twelve and Twelve explaining that the book dates from 1953 and why its text is kept.
background.cite: Advisory actions p2773, p2826, p2832, p2890 (M-39 pp. 94-98)

background.text: In 2021, on Literature committee recommendations, the Twelve and Twelve was edited on page 117 (“opposite sex” became “partner”) and on page 66 (a sentence now names the deadly sins of anger, lust or gluttony instead of severe examples), each with a footnote.
background.cite: 2021 Final Report pp. 60-61; advisory actions p3071, p3076

background.text: In 2022 the Conference Committee on Report and Charter, which had the item under a workload-sharing plan, took no action on moving “The Doctor’s Opinion” back to page one. It noted that Bill W. took part in repaginating the second edition and that other literature cites Big Book page numbers.

Requests to undo the 2021 edits have come back each year. A 2022 floor action to restore the original text was declined (the Conference voted not to consider it). In 2023 the trustees’ Literature Committee forwarded all such requests as one grouped item. From 2024 to 2026 it did not forward them: in 2024 it pointed to Fellowship sharing then under way on co-founders’ writings; in 2025 and 2026 it cited recent Conference discussion and no new information.
background.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 92; 2023 Final Report p. 92; 2024 Final Report pp. 97-98; 2025 Final Report p. 105; 2026 Final Report pp. 105, 107

background.text: The same trustees’ committee took no action in 2023 on a request to have scholars review the language of the story “Our Southern Friend,” noting that story selection belonged to the Fifth Edition subcommittee. In 2024 it took no action on an appendix of one-word spiritual principles, saying there is no one way to interpret them. In 2025 it took no action on restoring the electronic-meeting sentence, preferring to focus on the new Fifth Edition Foreword.
background.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 89; 2024 Final Report pp. 98-99; 2025 Final Report p. 106

background.text: The 2026 Conference approved the Fifth Edition, including 26 new stories, with minor editorial changes.
background.cite: 2026 Final Report pp. 5, 40; advisory action p3138

themes.now: The 1995 “remain as is” action on the Big Book’s first 164 pages and other core sections was cited again in 2021; in 2026 one Chapter 7 word was changed. Bill W.’s Twelve and Twelve text, kept as published in 2002, was edited in 2021 and 2026. Any change needs a two-thirds Conference vote, via committee or floor action.
themes.now_cite: Advisory actions p2773, p3069, p3139, p2826, p3071, p3076, p3135; Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 53, 60
themes.asked: Thirteen, all to the trustees’ Literature Committee. Twelve and Twelve: drop a phrase about women (38) or two Step Eleven phrases (85); undo 2021 edits (220). Big Book: inclusive language (36), “hundreds” to “thousands” (21), a footnote (94), Doctor’s Opinion to page one (142), restore a Foreword sentence (157), add a story or appendix (73, 200), change stories (69), review “To Employers” (180). All literature: no “He” for God (196).
raised: Some submitters say certain phrases are insulting or rest on old ideas about women who drink (38), or that gendered pronouns for God raise concerns (196). One (36) asks for inclusive language that keeps the original meaning.

Others ask to undo earlier edits: District 61 in Area 78 (220) wants about 80 requests sent since 2021 brought back and placed in the 2027 background, and others ask to restore the First Edition page numbering (142) or a removed Foreword sentence (157).
One submitter (21) says “hundreds” on page 51 was left over by mistake when the paragraph was changed in the second edition.
Supporters of additions say a footnote would give historical context (94) and that a list of principles could be a short study aid while allowing more than one interpretation (200).

considerations.text: The Conference’s stated reasons in 2021: the page 117 footnote gives context “as it relates to inclusivity,” and page 66 was revised to avoid examples “severe in nature.”
The Conference’s stated reasons for keeping wording: the preface already says the 1939 text is unchanged (1986), and the Fellowship wished Bill’s writings to be kept as originally published (2002).

Practical effects noted in the reports: repaginating would affect other literature that cites Big Book pages, and a change in English raises the question of matching changes in the Spanish and French books.
considerations.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 90; 2026 Final Report p. 48

considerations.text: When it declines to forward a request, the trustees’ Literature Committee often says there is no “widely expressed need” or no new information since the last discussion.
considerations.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 105-106; 2026 Final Report pp. 104-107

questions: For these two books, what weighs more for your group: keeping the original wording, or updating language for today’s readers? Are footnotes or an introduction a middle path?
Should the Big Book and the Twelve and Twelve be treated the same way?
When should an earlier edit (the 2002 Foreword sentence, the 2021 Twelve and Twelve changes) be looked at again, and what new information would justify it?
Where is the line between a correction, such as “hundreds” to “thousands,” and a change of meaning, and who should draw it?
Now that the Fifth Edition has new stories, how should requests about particular stories be handled?
themes.watch: Whether the trustees’ Literature Committee forwards any of these at the Oct 30 to Nov 2, 2026 board weekend, whether the 2021-edit requests are grouped as item 220 asks, and the Fifth Edition’s publication, expected early February 2027.

themes.name: Plain Language Big Book
themes.scope: Corrections, revisions, withdrawal, a new edition, side-by-side or cross-referenced versions of the Plain Language Big Book (PLBB, approved 2024), and the 2025 proposals deferred to this Conference.
themes.lede: The Plain Language Big Book (PLBB), “A Tool for Reading Alcoholics Anonymous,” puts the Big Book's text into plain and simple language. Approved by the Conference in 2024, it was published that November. In 2025 the Conference held proposals to rescind or revise it until this 77th Conference. This year's items seek withdrawal, revision, specific changes or new formats.

background.text: Earlier Conferences also worked on easier-to-read literature: in 1987 the Conference asked the trustees' Literature Committee to further explore the need for simplified material for people with limited vocabularies, and in 1989 it approved the illustrated, easy-to-read manuscript “Is A.A. for Me?” for people with limited reading skills.

A 2016 committee consideration of the 66th Conference suggested that the trustees' Literature Committee explore the need for “plain-language” recovery literature, which led to research subcommittees on access to the Big Book. Reporting to the 2021 Conference, the trustees' committee said a plain-language Big Book was not meant to replace the Big Book but to overcome barriers of relatability and access so the message might reach more alcoholics. That Conference then asked that a draft of the Big Book (Fourth Edition) be put into plain and simple language, accessible and relatable to as wide an audience as possible, with a progress report or draft in 2022.
background.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 31; 2021 Final Report pp. 46, 61 (Advisory Action p3097)

background.text: A trustees' Literature subcommittee formed in July 2021, Tools to Access the Big Book (TABB), oversaw the project with the Publishing Department; a writer was selected in February 2022 and contracted in May 2022. In 2023, after legal consultation, draft chapters were shown only to Conference members in a monitored reading room. That year's Conference Committee on Literature agreed with the project's general direction, and took no action on new proposals about it, acknowledging members' concerns about oversight of the process and pointing to a special session at that Conference.
background.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 63; 2023 Final Report pp. 32, 43, 89

background.text: In 2022 and again in 2024 the trustees' Literature Committee took no action on many proposals to stop, cancel, retitle or reshape the project, among them a side-by-side version and a request that A.A. members write it. In 2022 it noted that the Tools to Access the Big Book subcommittee oversaw the work; in 2024, that the project was in its final stages and that Conference procedures already provided for feedback on its direction.
background.cite: 2022 Final Report pp. 63–65; 2024 Final Report pp. 95–97

background.text: The 2024 Conference approved “Plain Language Big Book: A Tool for Reading Alcoholics Anonymous” with minor editorial changes: the Steps table became an appendix, and “addiction” and “addicted” were replaced with language about alcoholism. Floor actions to retitle it, to remove its explanations of the Steps, Traditions and Concepts, and to apply the Conference Committee on Literature's memo to the Publishing Department on remaining sticking points were sent back (recommitted) to the trustees. The trustees' Literature Committee later said the Conference had voted to keep the title.
background.cite: 2024 Final Report pp. 39, 52–53 (Advisory Action p3121); 2025 Final Report p. 107

background.text: Published November 1, 2024, the book's first printing of 72,500 copies sold out in two weeks. In its first 12 months 215,574 print copies were distributed and 7,789 e-books sold, and 2,240 e-book copies were accessed in the first 12 months it was offered on tablets in correctional facilities.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 15, 63; 2026 Final Report pp. 63–64

background.text: In 2025 the Conference decided that proposals to rescind or revise the book be collected and deferred to the 77th Conference “to allow for a wider Fellowship experience,” and called for a process within the trustees' Literature Committee to receive, assess and forward proposed changes. A floor action began a study of whether a plain-language Spanish Big Book or other tools would best help Spanish-speaking members.

Last cycle none of the six Plain Language Big Book proposals went to the Conference. Three (7, 86, 108; shown this year as 2025-7, 2025-86, 2025-108) were held for this Conference under the 2025 action. The trustees' Literature Committee took no action on the other three (a new title, 58; a review process, 60; an A.A. member as translator for changes, 43), pointing to its new change-process subcommittee, the 2025 deferral, or the Conference's role in approving changes. Three separate requests for a Spanish plain-language version (4, 71, 106) went to the subcommittee on plain-language tools in Spanish.

themes.now: The Plain Language Big Book remains Conference-approved; by its first anniversary it had four print runs and 322,000 copies in print, and no 2026 Advisory Action changed it. A trustees' Literature subcommittee is developing a process for proposed changes; the 2026 Conference Committee on Literature reviewed a progress report, asked for more detail and another report in 2027.
themes.now_cite: 2026 Final Report pp. 48–49, 63, 101; Advisory Actions (M-39) pp. 105–106
themes.asked: Fourteen items (three held over from 2025) ask to reconsider, withdraw or replace it (2025-7, 2025-86, 2025-108); suspend the first edition until a second is ready (60); revise it throughout (184); change passages such as the glossary's “craving” (1, 5, 13, 25, 141, 191); or tie it to the Big Book by facing pages, one volume or margin references (44, 113, 165). Items 92, 180, 185 also touch it.
raised: Item 13 asks that the glossary's definition of “craving” match how the Doctor's Opinion and the first 164 pages use the word, proposing “An irresistible physical urge to keep drinking once an alcoholic takes the first drink.” Item 5 asks for a correction of the same definition, in the glossary and at the end of the Doctor's Opinion.

Items 44, 113 and 165 each ask for a way to read the two books together: facing pages, one combined volume, or margin notes pointing to the original paragraphs. Item 113 says a combined book would make it easier to sponsor from.

Item 2025-86 describes the Plain Language Big Book as an interpretation and re-wording of the basic text, and item 184 speaks of the author's “nonalcoholic interpretation” of A.A.'s program of action. Items 2025-108 and 184 ask that a replacement or revision be done by a sober alcoholic or A.A. member with a deep understanding of the original text or of A.A. literature.

One submitter (92) proposes a different route: leave the Big Book itself unchanged for good and make any future revisions only in the Plain Language Big Book, which could then be updated as often as wanted.

considerations.text: Withdrawing the book or approving a revised edition would be a Conference decision: requests to change Conference-approved literature rise to the level of Conference action; a manuscript carries the Conference-approved label only when two-thirds of Conference members agree to it; and any action that affects an existing Advisory Action, such as the 2024 approval, also needs a two-thirds majority.

The 2025 Conference's stated reason for deferring these proposals was to allow a wider Fellowship experience with the book. In its report to that Conference, the trustees' Literature Committee took no action on proposals to stop, rescind or rework the book, one of them about how its Doctor's Opinion describes the physical side of alcoholism (the allergy or craving), saying the Fellowship should first have a chance to read it.

On formats, the Publishing Department noted (as reported in 2026) that the experts consulted on the book had advised against a side-by-side edition: the two texts would not line up word for word, and such a layout could make the book less useful to readers who struggle with the language of the first 164 pages. The 2026 Conference Committee on Literature separately suggested reference points to the matching Big Book pages and a page size like the large-print Big Book.

Answering a 2025 proposal that an A.A. member do the change work, the trustees' Literature Committee noted in 2026 that Conference members are consulted throughout the editorial process and must review and approve all changes, and that under Concept XI, when professional expertise is needed, A.A. World Services should hire the best possible consultants. The 2026 Conference Committee on Literature called the proposed agenda item (PAI) process the avenue for the Fellowship's suggested changes, and asked how many suggested changes are substantive and how many editorial.

questions: Has anyone in your group used the Plain Language Big Book, for example in a step study, with a sponsee or in corrections work? What was that experience like?
Should proposals to change specific passages (such as the glossary's definition of “craving”) be weighed separately from proposals to withdraw or replace the whole book?

Some proposals ask for facing pages, one combined volume or margin references to the Big Book. The experts consulted on the book advised against a side-by-side layout, and the 2026 Conference Committee on Literature suggested page references. Which, if any, would help readers in your group?
What review process for changes to the book would your group trust: yearly proposals through the agenda process, a standing review group, or something else?
Who should do the work of revising Conference-approved literature: A.A. members, hired professionals, or both, with the Conference approving the result?
themes.watch: At the Oct 30–Nov 2 General Service Board weekend, trustees' committees decide which proposals go to the 77th Conference; the November preliminary agenda should show how new and held-over items are handled. A change-process progress report is due in 2027.

themes.name: The A.A. Preamble
themes.scope: Wording of the A.A. Preamble (owned by the AA Grapevine): 'people' versus 'men and women' (changed 2021), 'particular faith', or asking the Fellowship's conscience on it.
themes.lede: The Preamble is the short statement of what A.A. is. It opens each Grapevine issue, and many groups read it at meetings. A Grapevine editor wrote it, and AA Grapevine, Inc. holds the copyright. In 2021 the Conference, through floor actions, replaced “men and women” with “people”. Members have since proposed changing it back, keeping it, or asking groups first.

background.text: The Preamble first appeared in the June 1947 issue of Grapevine. A Grapevine editor wrote it, borrowing phrasing from the foreword to the first edition of the Big Book.
background.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 181; 2025 Final Report p. 20

background.text: Earlier Conferences also looked at the wording. In 1966 a floor action kept the words “There are no dues or fees” in the Preamble, and in 1987 the Conference recommended that no changes or additions be made to it.

2020: the Conference committee on Grapevine took no action on a request to make the first sentence read “a fellowship of people”. It asked the Grapevine Board to consider drafting examples of gender-neutral wording, with a progress report or drafts for the 2021 Conference.

2021, in committee: the Grapevine and La Viña committee considered gender-neutral options and took no action, saying it needed more information. It asked the Grapevine Board to gather shared experience from the Fellowship and report to the 2022 committee.

2021, on the floor: late on the final day the Conference passed two floor actions. One reworded the opening to “In Alcoholics Anonymous we share…”, and the other replaced “men and women” with “people”. Since both had passed, a third floor action sent the “people” version to the General Service Board for approval as the new Preamble. The board accepted that year's Advisory Actions at its annual meeting.

2022: the trustees' General Service Conference Committee took no action on (did not forward) a proposal to stop printing the Preamble in A.A. World Services (AAWS) literature. It noted that many Advisory Actions approve literature that includes the Preamble and that the Preamble is a good introduction to A.A.

2023: the same trustees' committee did not forward a proposal to give the Preamble the special protection of Charter Article 3. It noted that the Preamble's copyright belongs to AA Grapevine and that it is not co-founder Bill W.'s writing.

2024: a floor action asked that the earlier proposals about the 2021 change be grouped and sent to a 2025 Conference committee, with a suggestion of wider discussion in the areas. It was recommitted (sent back) to the trustees' committees and boards along with other floor actions. 2025: the Conference declined to consider a floor action asking the board to make the “In Alcoholics Anonymous we share” wording the only Conference-approved Preamble.
background.cite: 2024 Final Report p. 52-53; 2025 Final Report p. 54

themes.now: Today's Preamble begins “Alcoholics Anonymous is a fellowship of people…” and carries an AA Grapevine, Inc. copyright line. It is not among the texts the Charter protects with three-quarters group consent (Article 12, the Steps and the Traditions). Last cycle a proposal with the same wording as #18 (item 76) went to the AA Grapevine Board and was not forwarded.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 3, p. 135; 76th Conference status grid (Feb 2026), item 76
themes.asked: Six proposals, all to the AA Grapevine Board. Three ask to restore “men and women” in place of “people” (#18, #59, #206). One asks that “people” stay (#205). One asks that groups, districts and areas be consulted on keeping the text, returning to pre-2021 wording or dropping any definition of the Fellowship, reporting in 2027 (#20). One asks to add “particular faith” to the non-alliance sentence (#56).
raised: The three submitters asking for “men and women” (#18, #59, #206) each make the request in one sentence. They describe it as restoring the earlier wording and give no other reasons in the grid.
The submitter of #56 says the words “particular faith” come from the Foreword to the First Edition of the Big Book, and asks for that language to be restored.
The submitter of #20 does not propose a wording. It asks that groups, districts and areas be consulted on three options and that a summary of their input come back to the 2027 Conference.
The submitter of #205 asks only that the word “people” remain.

considerations.text: How a change is decided: the Preamble is AA Grapevine's copyright, not one of the texts the Charter protects with three-quarters group consent. The usual path applies. A proposal goes to a trustees' committee, or to a board when the matter is the board's, which may refer it to a Conference committee. An Advisory Action approved by the Conference becomes binding when the General Service Board approves it. Floor actions can also bring up items that were not on the agenda.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 35, p. 60, p. 135, p. 182; 2026 Final Report p. 89

considerations.text: #20's request resembles two earlier steps on this topic: the 2021 committee's request for shared experience from the Fellowship, and the 2024 floor action asking for wider discussion in the areas. The Charter leaves delegates free to decide which questions to take to their groups for information, discussion or instruction.
considerations.cite: 2021 Final Report p. 66-67; 2024 Final Report p. 53; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 135

considerations.text: The Conference's own account of 2021 says members were committed to inclusive language. Two versions passed, and a third action recorded the Conference's preference for “people”. In 2022 the Grapevine and La Viña committee found it too early to measure the impact, because many members were still uninformed or ambivalent about the change.
considerations.cite: 2021 Final Report p. 5-6; 2022 Final Report p. 84

considerations.text: Practical effects: the revised Preamble was added to A.A. literature at each reprint in English, French and Spanish, including the Preamble placard and wallet card. Delegates' 2024 reports describe groups in Area 12 reading either version, as each group's conscience decides, and some meetings in Area 70 keeping “men and women”.
considerations.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 126, p. 133; 2024 Final Report p. 143, p. 146

questions: Which version of the Preamble does your group read, and how did the group decide?
Who should settle the Preamble's wording: the Conference, the AA Grapevine Board that holds the copyright, or the groups after being asked first?
If areas were asked for their conscience on the Preamble, as #20 proposes, how would your district gather and report it?
What would adding “particular faith” change in the sentence about what A.A. is not allied with?
Does the way the 2021 change was made (by floor actions on the last day of the Conference) matter to you, apart from the wording itself?
themes.watch: All six went to the AA Grapevine Board. After the fall board weekend (Oct 30 to Nov 2, 2026), watch the November preliminary 77th Conference agenda and the next status grid to see whether any is forwarded.

themes.name: Floor actions and late items should wait a year
themes.scope: Conference procedure: recommendations that were not on the agenda (floor actions, items a committee adds during Conference week) should be referred to the next year's agenda as proposed agenda items, or follow new guidelines, instead of being decided the same week.
themes.lede: A floor action is a recommendation made directly from the floor during the Conference's general sessions; it may not have gone through a Conference committee. Committees may also take up new items during the week. Most proposals here ask that such ideas wait a year so groups can discuss them first. Big Book-only versions mostly appear under Fellowship review.

background.text: 1968: When important questions could not be sent to the areas ahead of time, the Conference suggested presenting them orally early in the week, with discussion and voting later that week. The same year it asked that delegates be told of important issues so they could read prepared material and perhaps discuss it before voting.

1986: Speaking to floor actions proposed in the final hours of the Conference, the Conference reaffirmed the 1968 advice and added that matters of great significance, with a long-term effect on the Fellowship or substantial expense, raised in the waning hours should be referred to the appropriate committee at the next Conference so the group conscience is as informed as possible.

2018: The trustees' committee on the General Service Conference discussed the floor action process and had the service piece "How the Conference Operates" updated to clarify when floor actions may be introduced and to stress the value of submitting items by the Conference deadline, so they can go through the committee process.

2020-2022: The trustees' General Service Conference Committee forwarded to the Policy and Admissions Committee a proposal to review the floor action process "to guard against circumvention of the Conference process"; it was carried over to 2021. At the 2021 Conference a Policy and Admissions recommendation to replace the two-thirds motion to decline a floor action with a simple-majority motion to hear it won a simple majority but not two-thirds. The trustees' committee then took no action, noting it had a simple majority but not substantial unanimity.
background.cite: 2020 Final Report pp. 24, 61; 2021 Final Report p. 73; 2022 Final Report p. 33

background.text: 2024-2025: At the 2024 Conference one motion recommitted floor actions 5 to 15 to trustees' committees or boards without a decision; one of them (#9) asked that floor changes to founders' writings need 75%, then go to the areas for discussion before a final vote two Conferences later. Before the 2025 Conference, answering a 2024 Agenda Committee consideration about leaving more time for Conference business, the trustees' General Service Conference Committee updated "How the Conference Operates" and agreed with the idea of a decorum policy for floor actions. In 2025 there were twelve floor actions: one passed, nine were declined and two were recommitted, and the Conference closed at 11:47 p.m.
background.cite: 2024 Final Report pp. 52-53; 2025 Final Report pp. 5, 88-89

background.text: 2025: The Conference rescinded the 1986 rule that a committee recommendation with a majority but short of two-thirds "automatically becomes a suggestion." Such results, from a committee or a floor action, are not forwarded to the General Service Board for action; they are recorded in the Final Report for information and historical context (under their own heading since 2024).
background.cite: M-39 Advisory Actions pp. 125, 150, 163; 2025 Final Report pp. 38-39; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 43

background.text: Floor actions that became Advisory Actions: two in 2022, one in 2023 (a second was recommitted), one each in 2024 and 2025, and three in 2026: a higher suggested area contribution for delegate expenses, a print edition of the Final Report, and replacing "Eskimo" in the Tradition Eight essay of Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions. The matching Big Book change in 2026 was a recommendation of the Conference Committee on Literature, not a floor action. The 2026 Conference declined to consider a floor action to suspend printing the fifth edition of the Big Book until there was more consensus on procedures for changing founders' writings.
background.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 78; 2023 Final Report p. 36; 2024 Final Report p. 37; 2025 Final Report p. 37; 2026 Final Report pp. 39-40, 42

themes.now: Floor actions may be raised any time except Sharing Sessions, but anything within a committee's scope 'ought first' to go through that committee. The maker gets two minutes; the body may decline to consider it by a two-thirds vote. If heard, it needs two-thirds to become an Advisory Action; a simple-majority result is recorded in the Final Report only.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 42-43, 174-175 (Appendix W); p3711
themes.asked: Thirteen proposals (one a copy), with the trustees' General Service Conference Committee. Committee recommendations not on the agenda (#19, #117) or all committee motions (#172) would wait a year; passed floor motions go to a committee, then next year's agenda (#149, #171); new matters would start as proposals (#39, #78, #163, #178); #79 limits starting points; #32 defers Big Book floor changes; #213 seeks guidelines; #221 asks for a change.
raised: The submitters of #39 say broad participation and consultation strengthen an informed group conscience on matters of Fellowship-wide interest. They would allow same-week action only by a three-quarters vote on urgent matters that affect the service structure's ability to do its work (for example legal requirements, unforeseen financial risk, protecting A.A.'s assets or time-sensitive harm), and suggest that such exceptions not apply to literature, structure, governance or policy changes.

The submitters of #163 would apply the rule to every committee in the service structure: changes to literature, policy, procedure or structure would come only as a proposed agenda item, with background information, reviewed before the Conference meets.

The submitters of #213 focus on floor actions that would alter, replace or conflict with an earlier Advisory Action, and ask for a way for informed Fellowship input through the service structure before a final decision.

#149 (and its exact copy #171) would still let the Conference vote on floor motions, but a motion that passed would go to a committee and then onto the next year's agenda. #19 and #117 (committee recommendations not on the agenda) and #172 (any committee motion) would likewise move the decision to the next year; they give no further reasons in the grid.

considerations.text: When the trustees' General Service Conference Committee took no action on proposals for the 2022 Conference to change the floor action procedure and to require 80% to pass a motion (especially floor actions), it said the first request was similar to current practice, that the existing voting policy is effective and gives the minority a voice, and that an 80% threshold "would unduly limit the rights of the majority."

The Service Manual says Conference committees may take items as they are, modify them "and even consider new agenda items." A 2026 Inventory recommendation, committed (referred) to the General Service Board rather than decided, asked the Conference to acknowledge committees' authority to bring forward items not placed on their agenda or to defer an item to a future Conference.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 45; 2026 Final Report p. 42

considerations.text: How a change would be made: the floor rules are part of "How the Conference Operates," whose general rules are agreed to at the start of each Conference, and matters of policy need a two-thirds vote. The trustees' General Service Conference Committee has noted it has the purview to revise that document (it did so in 2018 and before the 2025 Conference). The Concept XII essay on Warranty Four says the Conference may agree in advance, by simple majority, what majority a particular question will need. A 2026 recommendation that non-editorial changes to the document go to Policy and Admissions a year before use did not reach two-thirds.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 42, 174, C-54; 2018 Final Report p. 78; 2025 Final Report p. 88; 2026 Final Report p. 42

considerations.text: A precedent: at the shortened virtual 2020 Conference, floor actions that were not declined were not voted on but went automatically to the trustees' General Service Conference Committee, which later sent them to trustees' committees (for example, a public service announcement aimed at minorities went to Public Information) or took no action.
considerations.cite: 2020 Final Report pp. 26, 54; 2021 Final Report pp. 24-25

questions: Which kinds of decisions, if any, should the Conference be able to make in the same week an idea is first raised, and which should wait a year for groups to discuss?

If floor actions and new committee items waited a year, what might be gained (time, background, group discussion) and what might be lost (urgent matters, a delegate's chance to act on what they hear that week)?
Who should decide whether a matter is urgent enough for an exception, and by what vote: a simple majority, two-thirds or three-quarters?
How does your group hear about decisions made from the Conference floor, and would earlier notice change how it takes part?
How do the Right of Appeal (Concept V) and the practice of hearing the minority after a vote fit with these proposals?
themes.watch: At the Oct 30-Nov 2, 2026 board weekend the trustees' General Service Conference Committee decides whether any reach the 77th Conference. Then watch the November status grid and the board's reply to the 2026 Inventory items on committee authority.

themes.name: Who sets the agenda; the Fellowship's voice
themes.scope: How the Conference agenda is set (committees vs the board), the share of Fellowship-submitted items, direct communication with or input from members, participation from outside the U.S./Canada structure, censure of a Conference, workshop topics about the Conference.
themes.lede: Who decides which proposals reach the Conference, and how members' views travel to it. Today the trustees' committees, hearing from Conference committees, usually choose what goes on the agenda. This year's proposals would give Conference committees a formal say, reserve room for Fellowship items, add direct channels to members, include people outside the U.S./Canada structure, or censure the 2026 Conference.

background.text: 1957: A floor action asked that the board's Policy Committee keep reviewing proposals sent in by delegates. If it felt one should not be sent out, the Conference Agenda Committee would review it; if that committee agreed to withhold it, the delegate would be told they were free to raise it on the Conference floor.

1995: After examining the issues and noting that communication had improved, the Conference Committee on Trustees unanimously recommended dismissing a proposal to censure the General Service Board, in the interest of A.A. unity and finding there was not sufficient cause; this became an Advisory Action.

2016-2018: A 2016 floor action asked the General Service Board for a plan giving area delegates a role in vetting and selecting proposed agenda items, and another action asked the General Service Office (GSO) to post the status of proposals on the Conference dashboard. In 2018 the Agenda Committee noted that one part of the plan, a call between each Conference committee and its trustees' committee chair before the January board weekend, had not happened and asked that it begin in January 2019. It also noted the board had reported no action on a request to keep considering a larger role for delegates in selecting agenda items.
background.cite: M-39 Advisory Actions p. 21; 2018 Final Report p. 50

background.text: 2018-2025: Floor actions on these subjects did not pass. Motions to censure the General Service Board were declined for consideration (2018), failed (2023) and were not approved after more than two hours of discussion (2025). Sending censure and reorganization proposals straight to the Conference Committee on Trustees was withdrawn as a floor action in 2018, and with no submission deadline was not approved in 2024. In 2025 the Conference declined to consider cutting standing agenda items to leave more room for Fellowship proposals, and giving the Agenda Committee the right of decision over the theme, presentations and workshops.
background.cite: 2018 Final Report p. 56; 2023 Final Report p. 50; 2024 Final Report p. 52; 2025 Final Report pp. 5, 54-55

background.text: 2025-2026: Under a 2025 Advisory Action, GSO sends Conference members a quarterly grid of every proposal and its status (first on Aug 20, 2025, then Nov 22, 2025 and Feb 6, 2026), with each motion printed in quotation marks exactly as submitted. The February 2026 grid for the 76th Conference lists seven proposals on agenda-setting and communication, among them a two-year wait before items reach the agenda, a joint vote of trustees' and Conference committee members on what makes the agenda, and background for the whole Fellowship by February 1 (items 24, 34 and 77 of that grid); none was forwarded.
background.cite: M-39 Advisory Actions p. 23; 2026 Final Report pp. 84-85; 76th Conference proposal status grid (Feb 2026)

background.text: 2026: Inventory recommendations that the Conference committed (referred) to the General Service Board included replacing the October feedback call with a joint meeting of trustees' and Conference committees in which all members have a voice and a vote on which proposals go forward. A plan for a nine-member working group to improve proposal selection did not reach two-thirds. The board had already decided that the incoming Conference committee chairs would attend the October board weekend instead of January, giving them longer to comment on proposals (the Service Manual still describes the January weekend).
background.cite: 2026 Final Report pp. 42, 50, 86; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 45

background.text: 2026: On the Agenda Committee's recommendation, the Conference set the 2027 theme, presentation topics and workshop topic. Proposed themes, workshops and presentation topics are reviewed by the Conference Agenda Committee.
background.cite: 2026 Final Report p. 39; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 46

background.text: 2026: The Conference asked the General Service Board to form an ad hoc committee, made up like the Conference (delegates, trustees, nontrustee directors and staff), to document how motions to censure or reorganize are received, considered and forwarded, and to propose ways of handling them that support unity, reporting to the 2027 Conference Committee on Trustees.

themes.now: Anyone may send a proposal; September 30 is the cutoff for the next April's Conference. The General Service Office's Conference coordinator suggests a route; trustees' committees usually decide 'when, where and whether' it reaches the agenda, after hearing their Conference committees. From October 2026 the incoming Conference committee chairs attend the fall board weekend where those decisions are made.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 43, 91, 171; 2025 Final Report p. 86; 2026 Final Report pp. 50, 87; p3707
themes.asked: Eight proposals: a formal role for Conference committees in setting their agendas (#16); at least two-thirds of agenda items from the Fellowship (#63, #98); a voice for people outside the U.S./Canada structure on changes to the founders' pre-1971 writings (#102); a study of an e-mail-type channel to members (#147) or member input through the contributions platform (#176); censure of the 2026 Conference (#58); a 'Right Size' workshop topic (#129).
raised: The Area 41 submission (#16) says Conference committees should have a formal role in setting their own agendas, rather than the General Service Board holding exclusive authority to set the Conference agenda.

Two submitters (#63, #98) want at least two-thirds of agenda items to come from the Fellowship (#98 calls it a goal for new items); #63 says that split would model the makeup of the Conference itself.

The submitters of #147 and #176 describe an opt-in channel (an anonymous e-mail-type system, or the new online contributions platform) that would let individual members hear directly about significant matters and give advisory, non-binding input.

#102 asks for a way for individuals, groups and others outside the U.S./Canada structure to take part when changes are proposed to the founders' writings from before 1971; #58 and #129 give no reasons in the grid.

considerations.text: When the trustees' General Service Conference Committee took no action on similar proposals for the 2022 Conference (sending proposed literature changes to every group; giving committees delegates' area consciences as background), it said groups and members already take part with a voice and a vote through their groups, districts and areas, and that ways to share already exist. On a request for worldwide participation in decisions on Bill W.'s writings, it noted that U.S./Canada actions may affect carrying the message worldwide but that the U.S./Canada board has no delegated authority to decide for groups internationally; it also noted there is no process to accept proposals from outside the U.S./Canada structure.

The Conference Charter says other countries have their own autonomous General Service Conferences, which rely on the Steps and Traditions protected by the U.S./Canada Conference; consultation between Conferences is encouraged, a World Service Meeting of their delegates is held every two years, and only matters seriously affecting A.A.'s worldwide needs are for joint consideration.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 124 (Current Conference Charter, Article 2)
