considerations.text: On direct channels to members: in its report to the 2025 Conference, the trustees' General Service Conference Committee noted that the proposal form is available to individual members on aa.org, and recorded concerns that wide online distribution of the form could lead members to bypass assemblies and the service structure.

On censure: this year's #58 was sent to the trustees' Nominating Committee, the counterpart of the Conference Committee on Trustees. The General Warranties (Concept XII) include that no Conference action ever be "personally punitive or an incitement to public controversy." In 2019 the trustees' committee on the Conference took no action on a proposal to send all censure or reorganization items straight to the Conference Committee on Trustees, saying the proposed agenda item process should be followed; in 2025-2026 a trustees' Nominating Committee subcommittee raised concerns that such routing could bypass the board's responsibilities under the Charter and does not adequately address the submitter's confidentiality.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 40, 48; 2019 Final Report p. 70; 2026 Final Report p. 109

questions: How does an idea from your home group reach the Conference today, and where, if anywhere, does it slow down?
Who should have the final say on which proposals reach the agenda: the trustees' committees, the Conference committees, or both together? What does Concept III's Right of Decision suggest to you?
Should a set share of the agenda be kept for proposals from the Fellowship, and what would that mean for standing items and reports from the boards?
Would a direct e-mail or app channel to individual members strengthen the group-district-area path, or work around it?
How should the Conference handle motions to censure, whether of the board or of a Conference, in light of the General Warranties?
themes.watch: At the Oct 30-Nov 2, 2026 board weekend (incoming Conference committee chairs now attend) trustees' committees decide what goes forward. Then watch the board's reply on the 2026 Inventory items and the censure-process report due at the April 2027 Conference.

themes.name: New and revised literature
themes.scope: New pamphlets, books, workbooks or study guides; revisions or audits of existing pamphlets and books other than the Big Book text itself (P-16 The A.A. Group, Living Sober, Daily Reflections, The God Word, Three Talks to Medical Societies, a Plain Language Twelve and Twelve, safety literature, etc.).
themes.lede: Proposals for new pamphlets, books and study tools, and for revising, auditing or reissuing existing pieces other than the Big Book text. Submitters name needs they see (grief, long-term sobriety, past abuse in Fourth and Fifth Step work), ask for Step workbooks, want the group pamphlet updated for online groups, and ask for older items in new formats.

background.text: Step study guides have been proposed before. In 1963 the Conference asked that a study guide to the Steps and Traditions, or a condensed Twelve Step book, be explored; in 1979 it set aside a Fourth Step pamphlet because the Big Book and the Twelve and Twelve cover the Step, and in 1985 it reaffirmed that Fourth and Fifth Step guides are not needed. In 2026 a request for a Twelve Step study guide or workbook reached the Conference; the committee that heard it (Finance, under the workload-sharing plan) took no action, noting such efforts exist locally, and the Conference declined to consider a floor motion on the same idea.

In 1977 the Conference dropped a proposed pamphlet called “Living Sober Longer” for lack of sufficient need. This year's long-term sobriety request (166) repeats, word for word, a 2026-cycle proposal that the trustees' Literature Committee did not forward; it said wider consultation would give more context on whether the need is widely expressed.

In 1985 the Conference asked A.A. World Services (AAWS) to produce A.A. Comes of Age on cassette; a CD album was still being distributed in 2025 (35 copies). In 2025 the Conference Committee on Treatment and Accessibilities suggested that the CD version be offered as an audiobook on aa.org.
background.cite: M-39 p. 89 (p2592); 2025 Final Report p. 52; 2026 Final Report p. 118

background.text: Living Sober was revised in 2012 to update outdated language and practices. In 2025 the Conference asked the trustees to update its language and content again; in 2026 the Conference Literature committee reviewed three revised draft chapters and suggested that the revisions continue in the same way.

In 2017 the Conference retired the pamphlet “Three Talks to Medical Societies by Bill W.” The trustees' Cooperation with the Professional Community (CPC) committee had said its language was dated and not helpful to today's communication about A.A., and noted that any retired piece stays available on request from the General Service Office (GSO) Archives for historical purposes.

In 2018 the Conference adopted Great Britain's pamphlet “The God Word,” with minor editorial changes, for A.A. World Services (AAWS) to publish. The Literature committee said adopting it answered the need expressed by atheist and agnostic members, and took no action on a request for a separate new pamphlet.

In 2020 the Conference accepted the A.A. World Services (AAWS) policy on keeping literature current, under which editorial updates are made; a 2025 request to change a Daily Reflections entry was answered by noting the change had already been made in 2022 under that policy. This year's Daily Reflections item (50) repeats, word for word, a 2026-cycle request that went to the AAWS board and was not forwarded to the Conference.
background.cite: M-39 p. 103 (p3067); 2020 Final Report p. 16; 2025 Final Report p. 105; PAI status grid for the 76th Conference (Feb. 2026)

background.text: In 2025 the trustees did not forward a request for a supplemental gender-neutral version of the Big Book's first 164 pages, saying the Fellowship should first have time to respond to the Plain Language Big Book. The same Conference decided that proposals to withdraw or revise that book be collected and held for the 77th Conference.

themes.now: New books and pamphlets usually start with a researched need, go through committee review of drafts and need approval by two-thirds of Conference members. The trustees' Literature Committee is updating Living Sober (revised draft or progress report due at the 2027 Conference) and developing pamphlets for Asian and Asian American alcoholics and for transgender alcoholics.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 77; 2026 Final Report pp. 48-49, 101-102
themes.asked: Fifteen items, plus two online-group items. New: grief (155), long-term sobriety (166), Steps Four–Five after abuse (68), Step workbook (29), Plain Language Twelve and Twelve (185), Steps by age (48). Revise: P-16 for online groups (96, 153), The God Word (6), Concepts Illustrated (24), pamphlet audit (31, copy 15), Daily Reflections (50), Living Sober (145), corrections (144). Reissue: Three Talks (177), Comes of Age audio (195), Advisory Actions (128).
raised: Several submitters describe needs they see as unmet: unaddressed grief as a factor in chronic relapse (155), the pitfalls of long-term sobriety (166), and how to work Steps Four and Five without taking responsibility for abuse done by others (68).
The submitters of 96 (Area 27, Louisiana) and 153 say the group pamphlet, “The A.A. Group” (P-16), should accurately represent and include online and hybrid groups.

The workbook proposals (29, and 182 in Spanish) ask for a structured Step study tool; 29 wants it sponsor-guided and attached a phased development plan. Item 31 asks for an audit of the pamphlets to find repetition and possible conflicts with the Traditions.

Item 177 wants Three Talks to Medical Societies reprinted with a cover note on the Lasker Award, to stress that alcoholism is a disease; item 145 wants the Living Sober revision to serve also as a public information and professional-outreach resource.

considerations.text: The Service Manual says the addition of a new book or pamphlet “is not approached lightly”: the need is usually researched first, and if it does not look urgent or broad enough the project is abandoned or deferred. Drafting can take months or years, and approval needs two-thirds of Conference members.

When the trustees' Literature Committee did not forward new-pamphlet ideas in the 2026 cycle, it said broad consultation is frequently useful and suggested sharing the idea in the district or area first (a pamphlet for Jewish members), said wider consultation would show whether a need is widely expressed (long-term sobriety), or pointed to existing AA Grapevine and La Viña resources (sponsorship).

The Conference already reviews a yearly Recovery Literature Matrix under an annual review plan in effect since 2017; in 2026 the Literature committee asked future matrixes to show more on the scope of revisions, copies distributed and which committee, staff member or department has purview over each piece. The General Service Office (GSO) Publishing Department reports that in 2025 revisions affected 25 to 60 A.A. World Services (AAWS) items a month.

The Literature committee's focus is recovery literature; material for a specific service area, such as corrections, is developed by that area's committee. In this grid the corrections pamphlet idea (144) went to the trustees' Corrections Committee and the Three Talks item (177) to the trustees' Cooperation with the Professional Community/Treatment and Accessibilities Committee.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 47; proposal grid for the 77th Conference (Oct. 1, 2026)

questions: What does our group already use for Step study, grief, or staying sober over many years, and does it meet the needs these proposals describe?
The trustees often ask whether a need is “widely expressed.” How could our group or district find out whether others share a need before sending a proposal?
Should a retired piece such as Three Talks to Medical Societies come back into print, stay in the Archives, or reappear in another form?
How should the Fellowship weigh new pamphlets against the work of keeping existing ones current?
What, if anything, should the group pamphlet (P-16) say about online and hybrid groups?
themes.watch: Trustees' committees and the A.A. World Services board decide around Oct 29–Nov 2, 2026 which items go forward (see the November status grid and preliminary agenda). A Living Sober draft or progress report is due in 2027.

themes.name: Spanish, French and other languages
themes.scope: Translations and language editions: the Spanish and French Big Books, Spanish-language study resources, publishing in all three languages at once, Marshallese, ASL.
themes.lede: Proposals about A.A. literature in languages other than English: a full review of the Spanish Big Book translation, new stories for the French Big Book, a translation into a Marshallese dialect, American Sign Language (ASL) versions of the Service Manual and three pamphlets, a Spanish Step workbook, and publishing English, Spanish and French versions at the same time.

background.text: Translation policy goes back to the 1950s. In 1958 the Conference asked A.A. Publishing to provide a basic A.A. book in other languages as needed, and in 1962 it adopted a long-range translation report: choose languages by how common alcoholism is among their speakers, and give the General Service Office (GSO) tighter control over translations of approved material.

In 2003 the Conference approved developing a Spanish Third Edition Big Book. The 2004 and 2007 actions set a complete review of the translated first 164 pages, Preface, Forewords, “The Doctor's Opinion,” “Dr. Bob's Nightmare” and Appendices for accuracy and consistent style and tone, with a bilingual story-selection subcommittee. The actions also noted that translations of Bill W.'s writings do not require Conference approval.

The 2019 keynote address, on the Big Book in 71 languages, recalled that three different Spanish translations had been in use and that the Spanish Third Edition went through a multinational review that included Mexico; it also said the first French translation (1952) covered the first 11 chapters and that French translations are now handled entirely through the General Service Office (GSO).

By the 2020 Conference, A.A. World Services (AAWS) had released the Big Book and the Twelve and Twelve in American Sign Language (ASL), saying the work answered an expressed need of the A.A. Deaf community, involved Fellowship input and was reviewed by Deaf members before publication. Both were still distributed on DVD in 2025.
background.cite: 2020 Final Report pp. 11, 15; 2026 Final Report p. 118

background.text: In 2021 the Conference began a Fourth Edition of the Spanish Big Book, Alcohólicos Anónimos, with updated stories. Progress reports went to every Conference from 2022 to 2026.
background.cite: M-39 p. 104 (p3085); 2022 Final Report p. 85; 2023 Final Report p. 43; 2024 Final Report p. 45; 2025 Final Report p. 46; 2026 Final Report p. 48

background.text: In 2022 the Conference asked that all Conference committee background be made available at the same time in English, French and Spanish. That year the Report and Charter committee asked the A.A. World Services (AAWS) board to research an American Sign Language (ASL) Service Manual; in 2023, after a feasibility report, it said materials should be translated in the order of the most widely expressed needs.
background.cite: M-39 p. 124 (p3692); 2022 Final Report p. 90; 2023 Final Report p. 47

background.text: A proposal in the 2024 cycle about which earlier French translation should be the base for the next French edition was sent by the trustees' Literature Committee to the A.A. World Services (AAWS) Publishing Department rather than to the Conference.

In 2025 a floor action started a study of Spanish-speaking members' needs, to decide whether a plain-language Spanish Big Book or other tools would better help readers facing literacy or comprehension barriers; a progress report is due in 2027. The same year, the Treatment and Accessibilities committee suggested that an American Sign Language (ASL) version of the group pamphlet (P-16) be prioritized.
background.cite: M-39 p. 105 (p3134); 2025 Final Report p. 52; 2026 Final Report p. 48

themes.now: A.A. World Services (AAWS) publishes Conference-approved items in English, Spanish and French. The Spanish Fourth Edition is in progress, with a manuscript or progress report due at the 2027 Literature committee. In 2026 the AAWS board affirmed that editions in other languages, Braille or American Sign Language are not translated back into English for Conference approval.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 76; 2026 Final Report pp. 17, 48
themes.asked: 8 items, 7 distinct wordings. A full review comparing the Spanish and English Big Books, reported in 2028 (162, 210; 212 copies 210). A Spanish Step workbook (182). New stories for the French Big Book (207). The Big Book in Ralik, a Marshallese dialect (65). American Sign Language (ASL) versions of the Service Manual and three pamphlets (51). Every new or revised piece in all three languages at once (3).
raised: The submitters of the Spanish review (162, 210, 212) want bilingual members, native speakers and translation staff to compare the Spanish and English texts for places where meaning, tone or the recovery message may not come through, so the new edition does more than update stories; 162 adds its view that the current Spanish book does not carry the core program and spiritual principles.
The French item (207) asks for new stories that better reflect today's French-speaking members, with a progress report in 2028.

Item 3 asks that any new or revised piece come out automatically in English, Spanish and French together. Items 51 (American Sign Language) and 65 (Marshallese) state the request without further reasons.
Item 182, submitted in Spanish with an English translation, asks for a Step study guide or workbook made for the Spanish-speaking community.

considerations.text: Translations of Bill W.'s writings do not need Conference approval, but the Conference has directed the Spanish Big Book projects: it approved developing the Third Edition in 2003 and producing it in 2007, and the Fourth Edition manuscript or a progress report is to come to its Literature committee in 2027.

On priorities, the 2023 Report and Charter committee said materials should be translated in the order of the most widely expressed needs. The General Service Office (GSO) reports that A.A. literature exists in 110 languages, that its departments work together to identify communities that need new translations, and that each translation is checked against the English original.
considerations.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 47; 2026 Final Report pp. 61, 95

considerations.text: On timing: in 2025 “The Twelve Steps Illustrated” came out in English in June and in French and Spanish in December, while the revised sponsorship pamphlet appeared in all three languages the same year. An A.A. World Services (AAWS) board committee has approved delivering key finance-related materials in all three languages at once whenever feasible.

In 2026 the Literature committee said more communication to the Fellowship about the Spanish Fourth Edition would help clear up misunderstanding, and suggested that a Spanish-speaking member of the Conference Literature committee take part in the final manuscript review. It also suggested considering the 2026 “Eskimo” change for the Spanish and French translations.

questions: Does anyone in our district read the Spanish or French Big Book or use American Sign Language (ASL) materials? What has their experience been?
Should a new or revised piece wait until all three languages are ready, or come out in English first so it is available sooner?
Who is best placed to judge whether a translation carries the message faithfully: bilingual members, professional translators, the Conference, or a mix?
How should A.A. decide which new languages or formats, such as Marshallese or ASL, come next?
themes.watch: Whether the trustees forward the Spanish review (162, 210, 212) or link it to the Spanish Fourth Edition, due in 2027 as a manuscript or progress report, and how A.A. World Services answers the sign-language, Marshallese and three-language requests.

themes.name: Online groups and a virtual area
themes.scope: Online/virtual groups in the service structure: a virtual area or forum, online groups in literature, how online groups contribute, reaffirming that areas are built from geographic groups.
themes.lede: Since 2021 the U.S./Canada structure has recognized online groups, which list with a district and area of their choice. This year's proposals return to questions the Conference and the board have taken up several times since: whether groups that meet only online, with no home geography, should have their own area and delegate, and how literature should describe them.

background.text: In 1997 the Conference agreed that online meetings asking to be listed would appear in the directories under 'International Correspondence Meetings,' with their web address and a member willing to be the mail contact.

In 2002 the Conference had a sentence deleted from future printings of the Big Book's Foreword to the Fourth Edition: that the difference between an electronic meeting and the home group around the corner is 'only one of format.' The committee noted that electronic meetings matter to some members. The trustees' Literature Committee took no action on requests to restore it, reported in 2023 (no widely expressed need) and 2025 (better to focus on the coming Fifth Edition Foreword).
background.cite: M-39 p. 96 (2002); 2023 Final Report p. 91; 2025 Final Report p. 106

background.text: The self-support pamphlet gained a question and answer on recurring online contributions in 2017, and one on passing a 'virtual' basket through digital payment platforms in 2020.

The 71st Conference (2021) recognized online groups and encouraged them to take part, listing each in the district and area it prefers (by default, where its primary contact lives) and replacing the 1997 label. It also asked the General Service Board to form a committee to explore how online groups could take part in the structure.

In 2022 the trustees' General Service Conference Committee took no action on six proposals about online groups (four for virtual or non-geographic areas, one to bring in online international groups, one to rescind the 2021 action) and sent their background to the board's ad hoc committee. On the international one it noted there is no process for proposals from outside the U.S./Canada structure. A floor motion asking for a plan for non-geographic areas did not become an Advisory Action.

The board's ad hoc committee reported 883 virtual group listings as of December 6, 2022 (587 with a general service representative as primary contact) and two virtual districts listed by the General Service Office, in Areas 48 and 72. One delegate's survey answer described an area that favored online groups taking part but had mixed feelings about whether a virtual area was the best answer.

In 2024 the Conference Committee on Policy and Admissions said the ad hoc committee's findings showed 'no clearly expressed needs' yet for an additional delegate area for online groups, and noted that a future guideline on online groups' participation might help. The service piece 'A.A. Guidelines for Online Groups' (MG-26) followed in 2025.
background.cite: 2024 Final Report p. 47; 2026 Final Report p. 91

background.text: In 2026 the Conference Committee on Archives (which had the item under the workload-sharing plan) discussed who may serve in area service while living outside the area. It took no action, noting the autonomy of areas and districts, and suggested that area-wide discussions continue on possible future linguistic and virtual areas.

themes.now: All 93 areas are geographic; there is no virtual area. Charter Article 5 makes each area assembly out of the general service representatives, district committee members and area officers of a delegate area. Each group names a preferred district and area; for online groups this varies, since they are non-geographic, and some areas have virtual districts.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 14, 117, 125
themes.asked: Eight proposals touch this theme. Structural: a new area for online-only groups (#22); a virtual area with its own districts, assemblies and delegate (#112); reaffirming Charter Article 5 on who forms area assemblies (#183). Others: 'The A.A. Group' pamphlet to cover online and hybrid groups (#96, #153); self-support text on contributions from online and clubhouse meetings (#105); restoring the Foreword sentence deleted in 2002 (#157); an online Special Forum (#156).
raised: #22 describes groups that meet only online and are not tied to any existing area; #112 would give online groups virtual districts, assemblies and a delegate with the same duties as other delegates.

Area 27 (#96) asks for a review so that online groups are accurately represented in what it calls foundational literature; #153 puts information for online and hybrid groups first and other changes second.
Area 51 (#156) proposes the online Special Forum mainly for members of online groups that are not part of any of the eight regions.
#105 asks self-support literature to explain how online and clubhouse meetings can contribute, both to the General Service Office and to the conscience of A.A.

considerations.text: A request for a new delegate area goes through a General Service Office application that asks mainly about geography, A.A. population and how well the existing area structure works. A 1961 memo from Bill W. quoted there says the Conference is not a political body needing a rigid formula of representation, but needs enough delegates for a reliable cross section of A.A. and good local communication.

Requests to create additional delegate areas or otherwise expand the Conference go to the Conference Committee on Policy and Admissions; changes to the Charter, such as Article 5, are reviewed by the Committee on Report and Charter.

The 2023 ad hoc committee report summarized hopes raised in international sharing at the World Service Meeting (reaching remote areas, more young people, savings from holding service meetings online) and concerns (less contact after meetings, less interest in service, privacy, Seventh Tradition), and said the question remains of groups with no geographic 'tether' and how to keep unity.

Groups ask the office what to do when members live in other countries. In 2022 the trustees' General Service Conference Committee noted the U.S./Canada board has no delegated authority to decide for groups internationally. The group listing form suggests virtual groups based outside the U.S./Canada contact their own country's office, and says groups based outside, or with no geographic location, may contact the General Service Office's International desk.
considerations.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 28; 2022 Final Report p. 41; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 117

questions: Does your group, or an online group you attend, take part in general service today? Through which district and area?
What would a separate virtual area add, and what might change for geographic areas such as Area 65 and its districts?
Should 'The A.A. Group' pamphlet say more about online and hybrid groups, and if so, what?
How do the online meetings you know pass the basket, and should literature say more about it?
Bill W. wrote that the Conference needs a reliable cross section of A.A.; how should groups with no geographic home be part of that?
themes.watch: At the October 30–November 2, 2026 board weekend the trustees' General Service Conference Committee decides on #22, #112 and #183, and the Literature, Finance and Conventions/Forums committees on the others. The preliminary agenda follows in November.

themes.name: Service Manual and the Concepts
themes.scope: Text of The A.A. Service Manual / Twelve Concepts for World Service: restoring removed passages (Concept XI, the group definition), footnotes, proxies at assemblies, adding the 2022 reorganization procedure.
themes.lede: The A.A. Service Manual, bound with Bill W.'s Twelve Concepts for World Service, comes out every two years under Conference oversight. This year's proposals would restore removed text (two Concept XI paragraphs, the group definition), add footnotes or an appendix, change a district answer on who votes at assemblies, and change one word in an illustrated Concepts pamphlet.

background.text: In 1964 a show of hands on the Conference floor found the sense of the meeting against proxy voting by general service representatives at area assemblies, as open to abuse, while recognizing that groups in correctional institutions and some hospitals might otherwise go unrepresented.

The Conference added 'What Is an A.A. Group' to the Service Manual in 1989, replaced its six-point group description with the long form of Tradition Three plus part of Warranty Six in 1991, and in 2000 added that description to Chapter Two, 'The Group and Its G.S.R.' (the group chapter is Chapter 1 in today's edition).

The 66th Conference (2016) removed two paragraphs about women workers from the Concept XI essay and had the endnote say they remain available from the General Service Office Archives as historical reference.

Requests to reconsider met no action: the trustees' Literature Committee in 2017 cited faith in the committee process and the informed group conscience behind the 2016 action; the trustees' General Service Conference Committee in 2019 saw no widely expressed need; and in 2020 the Conference Committee on Report and Charter found the archives endnote adequate.
background.cite: 2017 Final Report p. 59; 2019 Final Report p. 71; 2020 Final Report p. 59

background.text: In 2021 the Conference asked for an 'Amendments' section at the end of the Concepts with an updated Concept XI essay; the 76th Conference (2026) approved it. In the 2026-2028 edition that section reprints the two removed paragraphs as part of the record, along with the original wording behind a 2025 one-word change to the Concept IV essay.
background.cite: 2021 Final Report p. 63; 2026 Final Report p. 40; Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. C-61, C-74

background.text: In 2022 the Conference approved a 'Suggested Procedure to Reorganize' the General Service Board and the A.A. World Services and AA Grapevine boards as one acceptable pathway, leaving the final process to whichever Conference considers a reorganization.

In 2025 the Conference rescinded a 1986 action that made majority-but-not-two-thirds recommendations into suggestions; such results are now recorded in the Final Report for information and historical context, not as suggestions to the board.

In 2026 the Conference asked the board to form an ad hoc committee, made up like the Conference, to document how motions to censure or reorganize are received, considered and forwarded, and to report to the 2027 Conference Committee on Trustees.

themes.now: In the 2026-2028 edition, Chapter 1 opens with the home group and the general service representative's role, without the group-definition passage; Tradition Three's long form is on pp. 106 and 117. The district chapter says only the elected district committee member, or the alternate when absent, may vote at area meetings. Concept XI's endnote mentions the removed paragraphs.
themes.asked: Seven proposals, six distinct: a written proxy, signed by two members, for a district with no district committee member or alternate (#9); re-insert two Concept XI paragraphs in revised form (#64); restore the group definition to Chapter 1 (#125; #135 copies it); footnote Concept V on trustees and simple majorities (#192); add the 2022 reorganization procedure as an appendix (#67); replace 'investing' in the illustrated Concepts pamphlet (#24). Related: #175.
raised: #125 and #135 point out that 1991 and 2000 Advisory Actions placed the group-definition passage in the group chapter, and ask that it return right after Chapter 1's first paragraph.
The submitter of #24 says A.A. does not invest, so a word such as 'managing' would fit better in the illustrated pamphlet's Concept VI text.
#9 would let a member appointed by two other members, through a written and signed proxy, represent at an assembly a district that has neither a district committee member nor an alternate.

#67 asks for a footnote in Concept III pointing readers to the reorganization procedure; #192 asks a Concept V footnote to clarify the trustees' role when a recommendation reaches only a simple majority.

considerations.text: Bill W. wrote in the introduction to the Concepts that those seeking structural change 'need only make out a strong case' that convinces both trustees and Conference, and suggested that a far-reaching change, once finally approved, be entered in an 'Amendments' section so the original text stays as a record.

The Conference Committee on Report and Charter reviews the Service Manual and recommends changes, and reviews any needed Charter changes. The manual comes out every two years, with the three boards sending updates in printing years.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 47; M-39 pp. 161-163 (actions p4761, p4777, p4795)

considerations.text: The manual leaves assembly voting practices to each area: among questions an assembly might take up, it asks whether general service representatives may vote by proxy, and notes that proxies are used in some areas but are not a common practice.

Of last year's five Service Manual proposals (items 9, 69, 79, 105 and 110 of that grid), only item 9, on removing a Dr. Bob quote, reached the agenda; the Conference Committee on Report and Charter took no action on it. Item 69 had asked, as #175 does now, for the manual free in service kits. The committee also said margin change bars are no longer needed and suggested a list of changes at the front of the book.
considerations.cite: Proposal grid for the 76th Conference (Feb 2026); 2026 Final Report p. 51

questions: Should the Service Manual set one answer on proxies at assemblies, or leave it to each area's practice? What does Area 65 do?
When the Conference removes text from Bill W.'s writings, where should it be kept: in the essay, in an Amendments section, or in the Archives?
The long form of Tradition Three already appears elsewhere in the manual; does it also belong at the start of Chapter 1?
Would footnotes on Concepts III and V help your group study the Concepts?
themes.watch: Most of these went to the trustees' General Service Conference Committee (#67 to Nominating, #24 to Literature), deciding at the October 30–November 2, 2026 board weekend. The 2027 Committee on Trustees receives the report on censure and reorganization procedures.

themes.name: Boards, offices and the Conference itself
themes.scope: Size and makeup of the General Service Board, regions, rotation rules for trustee and director candidates, consolidating Conference committees, a new corporate board, moving GSO, holding the Conference online.
themes.lede: These proposals would change how the service structure is built: the number of trustees and regions, waiting periods between board roles, the number of Conference committees, a new corporate board, where the General Service Office sits, and whether the Conference sometimes meets online. Two of them repeat ideas from last year that did not reach the agenda.

background.text: The first Conference year (1951) began with eight nonalcoholic (Class A) and seven A.A.-member (Class B) trustees, most living near New York. The board grew in 1962 to bring in A.A. trustees from farther away, and in 1966 took its present form of 7 Class A and 14 Class B trustees.
In 1956 the Conference tabled, for some future date, a proposal to hold the Conference in New York City in even years and elsewhere in odd years.
In 1978 the Conference asked the board to study restructuring the regions; in 1979 it accepted a statement advising no restructuring at that time.

In 1994 the Conference declined to form a committee to move the General Service Office out of New York, as not financially prudent and not needed at the time. Relocation studies have been made about every ten years; after the Location Plus study begun in 2022, consultants advised staying, and in October 2023 the board decided to renew the office lease in Manhattan.

The 2020 Conference met online for the first time, after the board decided not to meet in person in New York, and handled only essential business; 2021 was also virtual. In 2021 the trustees' General Service Conference Committee called a proposed ten-year trial alternating in-person and virtual Conferences premature after only one virtual experience; in 2022 it took no action on a similar request, while supporting virtual tools within in-person Conferences to save costs.
background.cite: 2020 Final Report p. 4; 2021 Final Report pp. 4, 28; 2022 Final Report p. 39

background.text: In 2017 the Conference asked for a plan to spread committee workload more fairly by combining or creating committees. The Equitable Distribution of Workload process that followed was set in 2021 as a three-year trial starting with the 2022 Conference, adopted in 2024, and in 2026 the Conference voted to end it after the 78th Conference (2028).

In 2026 the Conference Committee on Policy and Admissions took no action on giving each committee a similar number of items regardless of topic, or on creating a Conference digital committee, citing little evidence of efficiency gains and the extra work and staff a new committee would need; it called for a more comprehensive approach to workload.

The 2026 Conference Committee on Finance asked the general manager, the trustees' General Service Conference Committee and the office's meetings and travel team to keep exploring cost-saving options for the Conference, including a hybrid online and in-person (New York City) format, with a progress report to the 2027 Finance committee.

themes.now: The board has 21 trustees: 7 Class A (nonalcoholic) and 14 Class B (A.A. members: 8 regional, 4 general service, 2 at-large), with 8 regions (6 U.S., 2 Canada). The Conference has 13 standing committees, including two secondary ones. Charter Article 9 says the Conference meets yearly in New York unless otherwise agreed.
themes.asked: Six proposals: a 33-member board, 16 regions (22 Class B, 11 Class A) (#75); a one-year break from Conference or board service before nontrustee director or general service trustee posts (#17); one District and Intergroup Support Committee replacing four (#103); a third corporate board for social media (#104); moving the General Service Office to Akron, Ohio (#61); an online Conference every other year (#194). Related: #22, #112, #183, #67, #129.
raised: #75 says its numbers keep the board's two-thirds to one-third balance between A.A.-member and nonalcoholic trustees.
The submitter of #104 notes the idea was sent last year without trustee action, and links it to the committee consolidation proposal as an answer to Conference workload.
#103 says the merged committee would take up new agenda items and keep reviewing kits and workbooks; it leaves digital media out of the Public Information part.
#194 says meeting online in alternate years would cut Conference costs, and mentions the size of the reserve.

considerations.text: The board's bylaws now fix 21 member trustees. They can be amended by 75% of all trustees, or by a majority of trustees present once the change has gone to the Conference delegates and a majority has not disapproved; the board is expected, though not legally required, to submit changes to the delegates. The Charter adds that, by tradition, such changes should have two-thirds approval of all Conference members. Delegates are meant to remain at least two-thirds of the Conference's voting members.

Last year the trustees' Nominating Committee took no action on two waiting-period proposals, citing the need to fill director and general service trustee vacancies by the skills the corporations need, and the continuity and large candidate pool the general service trustee selection needs; general service trustees are chosen from current or past nontrustee directors.
considerations.cite: 2026 Final Report p. 110; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 56

considerations.text: The Charter already speaks of 'such other service corporations as the Conference may desire to form,' placing them, like A.A. World Services and AA Grapevine, under the board's responsibility for financial and policy integrity.

In 2025 the trustees' Finance Committee took no action on setting aside funds for a future move out of New York; it said the idea had merit but cited the more pressing need to rebuild the Reserve Fund and the existing practice of a relocation study every ten years.

questions: Regional trustees bring a regional point of view to the board without representing a region; what would more, smaller regions mean for the Southwest Region and Area 65?
Should someone leaving one board or Conference role wait a year before taking another, as a delegate does before standing for trustee?
How would one combined Conference committee for corrections, treatment and accessibilities, professional cooperation and public information affect the service committees in your district?
What would be gained, and what lost, if the Conference met online in some years?
Does the location of the General Service Office matter to your group? Why?
themes.watch: Trustees' committees, the General Service Board (#75, #104) and the A.A. World Services board (#61) decide at fall 2026 meetings (board weekend October 30–November 2). A Conference cost-saving report, including a hybrid format, is due to the 2027 Finance committee.

themes.name: Money: reserve fund, spending and transparency
themes.scope: Reserve Fund minimums and replenishment, use of reserve income, disclosure of large purchases and agreements, GSO staffing costs, prices and free copies, Grapevine self-support and print costs, self-support literature.
themes.lede: Proposals about A.A.'s money at the national level: how large the General Service Board's Reserve Fund (the Fellowship's prudent reserve) should be and what happens when it runs low, how much members are told about large purchases, what the General Service Office spends on staff, and what literature and service books cost.

background.text: The board of trustees set up the Reserve Fund in 1954. Its purpose is to keep the services of A.A. World Services (AAWS) and AA Grapevine going in an emergency, to pay costs beyond their means such as major leasehold improvements or technical upgrades, and to give the boards time to adjust to changed conditions.
In 1967 the Conference agreed that the General Service Board may use the Reserve Fund's investment income for whatever purpose the board authorizes. Item #179 asks to revise this action.

In 1977 the Conference set the prudent reserve equal to the previous year's combined operating expenses of the three corporations, with the auditors commenting each year on its adequacy. In 1987 it changed "equal to" to "not to exceed" and decided not to set a lower limit, because the auditor must comment on whether the fund is adequate.

Since 2001, if the fund goes above the 12-month limit, one year is allowed to review its level and a second year to plan how to bring it back under the limit. The Service Manual describes no matching step for a fund that falls low.

In 2022 the General Service Board adopted its own Reserve Fund policy, which sets a goal range of 9 to 12 months of operating expenses, keeps at least half the portfolio available within a year, and requires board authorization for transfers in and out. The Service Manual's questions-and-answers section likewise describes the fund as covering nine months to a year of combined expenses.
background.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 21; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 69

background.text: The Conference asked for more quarterly reporting of the three boards' finances (2023) and for capital projects and maintenance costs to be added to the Quarterly Financial Report (2025). By 2026 that report ran to more than 50 pages and included Reserve Fund information; delegates hold copies.

In March 2025 the AAWS board adopted a literature price review policy: when the reserve is low, prices may rise to protect it; when it is high, prices may hold or fall. In December 2025 the AAWS board approved a price increase of $3 per book and 15% on other items from February 1, 2026.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report pp. 18-19; 2026 Final Report p. 14

background.text: In 2025 contributions were $10.579 million, 6% less than 2024, and slightly more than a third of active groups contributed. Personnel costs were 65% of the General Service Office's operating expenses. The Reserve Fund fell to $11.022 million (6.17 months of 2025 expenses) after $1.25 million in drawdowns and $354,549 in investment earnings, and was projected at 4.79 months by the end of 2026 after office-retrofit drawdowns.

themes.now: The Conference caps the Reserve Fund at one year's operating expenses and has set no minimum; the board's 2022 policy aims for 9 to 12 months. On December 31, 2025 it held $11.02 million, about 6.2 months of 2025 expenses, projected near 4.8 months by end of 2026. The A.A. World Services board calls returning to that range a priority.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 65; p1333; 2023 Final Report p. 21; 2026 Final Report pp. 14, 26
themes.asked: Twelve proposals; five on the Reserve Fund: refilling it after a year below target (#133), a three-month floor (#134), income use only above six months (#179), a nine-month minimum (#181), a Conference session on rebuilding (#109). Others: disclosure of large purchases (#77, #169) and the Everything AA app's cost (#35), a staffing review (#49), self-support wording for online and club meetings (#105), one print-and-digital price (#127), free Service Manuals (#175).
raised: Item #133 points to the 9-to-12-month range in the board's October 2022 Reserve Fund policy; #181 says nine months is the minimum the board has used for many years and notes the Conference has already set a 12-month maximum.

Item #134 would set a three-month minimum: after two quarters below it, the board would report a recovery plan to the Conference Committee on Finance, then an updated plan each year until the fund reaches 4.5 months. Item #179 would let the board use reserve income only while the fund holds at least six months.

Items #77 and #169 present their requests as transparency with the Fellowship: #77 about asset purchases over $500,000, with nondisclosure agreements strongly discouraged; #169 about significant acquisitions and commitments, including digital assets, while protecting information that is legitimately confidential.

Item #49 asks that office staffing and personnel spending match current and projected finances. Item #127 asks for every communication in print and electronic form at one price, postage-free; #175 asks that the Service Manual come free in the kits for general service representatives (GSRs) and district committee members (DCMs), and #128 that delegates get a free printed, updated Advisory Actions booklet (M-39).

considerations.text: The Conference's own reason for having no lower limit: in 1987 it chose not to set one because the auditor is required to comment each year on whether the fund is adequate.

Last cycle the trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee took no action on two similar proposals (a limit on how reserve income may be used, and a nine-month refill plan), saying such a policy might restrict the board from fulfilling its legal responsibilities; it favored a broader Conference session on "Rebuilding Our Reserve Fund" instead. The 2026 Conference Finance committee also asked the Agenda committee to consider a 2027 workshop or theme on the Reserve Fund.

On last cycle's request for fuller financial disclosure, the trustees' committee said existing annual and quarterly reports suffice, that more detail would overburden staff, that confidentiality must be kept, and that the Quarterly Financial Report had recently been expanded. The 2026 Conference Finance committee worried that detailed reports on aa.org might cause confusion and suggested brief, easy-to-read snapshots of A.A. finances and self-support instead.

Who decides: the 12-month limit was set by Conference action, while the board, on its Finance and Budgetary Committee's recommendation, authorizes withdrawals. The Conference Committee on Finance can review or start recommendations that involve finances.

questions: What should a prudent reserve mean for A.A. as a whole: only an upper limit, or a floor as well?
If the fund stays below its target, who should act, and how should groups hear about the plan?
How much financial detail helps our group understand where its contributions go, and when does detail become too much?
How do our group's contributions and literature purchases connect to the Reserve Fund and to literature prices?
Should service books for general service representatives (GSRs), district committee members (DCMs) and delegates be free, and how would that cost be covered?
themes.watch: At the fall board weekend (Oct 30-Nov 2, 2026) the trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee, the A.A. World Services board (#35, #49, #127, #175) and trustees' Conference committee (#109) respond. Last cycle 1 of 9 money proposals went forward.

themes.name: Apps, AI and technology
themes.scope: The Everything A.A. app (cost, content), Meeting Guide, an A.A. AI tool, outside platforms, digital member communication tools.
themes.lede: Proposals about the digital tools that A.A. World Services runs or might take on: the Everything AA app, outside meeting-finder platforms, an A.A.-run artificial intelligence (AI) tool, and ways for the General Service Office to reach individual members directly and hear back from them.

background.text: In 2004 the Conference set how the A.A. website is overseen: A.A. World Services (AAWS) manages aa.org and reports quarterly and yearly to the trustees' Public Information Committee, and major changes may involve consultation.

In 2013 the Conference allowed AAWS to sell and distribute digital literature through apps, e-readers and online stores, with protective contracts and a report back; Grapevine had received similar permission in 2011.
In 2023 the Conference asked the AAWS board to give the trustees' and Conference public information committees regular analytics on its communication platforms.

In 2025 the AAWS board adopted a policy on appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI): no AI tools where sensitive identifiable personal information is involved, accuracy checks, and regular review as the technology changes.

AAWS's 2025 planning tool listed technology work (an "AAWS App", hardware and analytics) at $932,000 among the "year 2 possibilities" for 2026. That year the Conference Literature committee discussed the need for an app to sell digital literature, took no action, and looked forward to more information on current efforts.

In the 76th cycle (2026) a proposal for an A.A. app holding all literature, or the purchase of the existing Everything AA app, and one on Meeting Guide data went to the AAWS board and were not forwarded to the Conference.
background.cite: 76th Conference PAI status grid (Feb. 2026), items 35 and 66

background.text: The Service Manual now lists the Everything AA app, with aa.org and Meeting Guide, among the platforms overseen by the AAWS board's Services and Technology committee. The 2025 and 2026 Final Reports do not name the app or report a purchase price; the 2026 capital budget includes $30,000 for an "AAWS App High Level Design".
background.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 66; 2026 Final Report p. 145

background.text: In 2025-2026 Meeting Guide added an Online Meetings view, the trustees' Public Information Committee began exploring push notifications, a communications working group's report to the board suggested considering an app with notifications to centralize communications, and an AAWS committee discussed opt-in outreach at events and alternative platforms for online contributions.

themes.now: The A.A. World Services (AAWS) board's Services and Technology committee oversees AAWS technology and digital services, including aa.org and the Meeting Guide and Everything AA apps. The 2025-2026 Final Reports do not mention Everything AA by name. The Charter expects the Conference to give a reliable cross-section of A.A. opinion, and any member may propose an agenda item.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 43, 66, 124
themes.asked: Six proposals: disclose what the Everything AA app cost (#35); keep a recorded workshop on the app (#55); review an outside meeting-finder platform (#47); explore an A.A.-controlled, privacy-centered artificial intelligence (AI) tool (#110); and two direct links to members: a board study of a voluntary, anonymous e-mail system (#147) and using the contributions platform for news and non-binding input (#176). Meeting Guide listings (#214) appear under Safety.
raised: Item #110 asks that any A.A. AI run on open-source software that A.A. hosts itself, protect anonymity and privacy, and offer information only, never taking the place of sponsors, meetings, professional help or human contact.

Item #147 seeks a study of a voluntary, anonymous e-mail-type system through which individual members could hear directly about significant Fellowship matters and give advisory input to the office and the service structure; #176 would use the contributions platform to tell participating members about significant actions and collect their non-binding input.

Item #47 says the outside platform it describes helps members find the actual meeting room, not only the building; #35 asks how much was spent acquiring the Everything AA app, and #55 asks that a recorded workshop now on the app stay available as it is.

considerations.text: Who decides: the A.A. World Services (AAWS) Social Media Policy reaffirms that operational decisions stay with the General Service Office and AAWS, and an AAWS committee is reviewing where authority for website updates lies among office administration, the AAWS board and Conference oversight.

Discussing outside platforms for online contributions in 2026, an AAWS committee acknowledged that AAWS is not a software developer, noted that customizing outside platforms can reduce their cost-effectiveness, and stressed open-mindedness about using existing external platforms while keeping any AAWS-created content consistent with A.A. principles.

The AAWS policy on artificial intelligence (AI) already bars AI tools where sensitive identifiable personal information is involved and calls for accuracy checks. In 2026 the trustees' General Service Conference Committee noted that a suggested use of open-source AI (to help assign delegates to committees) does not align with that policy, while an AI interpretation platform used at the 2025 Regional Forums was judged an effective way to provide interpretation.
considerations.cite: 2025 Final Report p. 13; 2026 Final Report pp. 83, 98

considerations.text: Under the Conference Charter, delegates are free to decide which questions to take to the group level. The AAWS committee discussing opt-in outreach stressed attention to privacy and compliance.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 124; 2026 Final Report p. 17

questions: Which A.A. digital tools does our group use, and what would we want to know about what they cost?
Where should the line fall between the office's day-to-day technology decisions and matters for the Conference?
What anonymity and privacy safeguards would members want before A.A. uses AI tools or a member e-mail list?
Should individual members be able to give input directly to the office, or should input keep going through the group's general service representative, the district and the delegate?
When an outside company offers a tool for A.A. members, what should A.A. weigh before working with it?
themes.watch: The A.A. World Services board (and, for #147, the General Service Board) responds around the fall board weekend, Oct 30-Nov 2, 2026. A progress report on Meeting Guide push notifications is due to the 2027 Public Information committee.

themes.name: Public information and outreach
themes.scope: Videos, PSAs, public information pieces, social media guidance, membership estimates, the Tradition Eleven short form and the internet, corrections and professional outreach pieces.
themes.lede: Proposals about how A.A. presents itself to the public and to professionals: videos and public service announcements (PSAs), social media, published membership numbers, the wording of Tradition Eleven's short form, and literature for carrying the message into correctional facilities.

background.text: In 1958 the Conference left group membership counts to the groups, urging inclusive counts, and asked delegates to stress the need for accurate census figures in their area reports.
In 1974 the Conference kept the wording of Tradition Eleven unchanged and asked delegates to explain that television is implied in its last phrase, "press, radio, and films."

The film "Hope: Alcoholics Anonymous" was accepted in 1990 to meet a need expressed by members carrying the message into treatment facilities, with French and Spanish versions and captions; a revision keeping only the script was asked for in 2007 and approved in 2009.
In 2013 the Conference affirmed that the internet, social media and all forms of public communication are implicit in the last phrase of Tradition Eleven's short form.

The 2022 Final Report was the last to print "Estimates of A.A. Groups and Members" (as of December 31, 2021: 71,138 groups and 1,474,958 members in the U.S. and Canada, based on reports from groups listed with the General Service Office (GSO), not an actual count). The 2023 report's contents page no longer lists it; GSO now lists the estimates among the reference material it keeps up to date.
background.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 108; 2023 Final Report p. 3; 2026 Final Report p. 91

background.text: In 2024 a Conference committee reviewed the Hope video and took no action, finding its information still relevant and the video still useful, and that updating it would not be prudent at that time.

In 2025-2026 the Conference set a five-year review cycle for video public service announcements (PSAs), approved a revised anonymity pamphlet covering social media (retitled "Anonymity – Our Spiritual Foundation"), and approved a pilot membership survey testing ways to reach groups not registered with the General Service Office.

On last cycle's proposals, the trustees' Public Information Committee took no action on adding "and social media" to Tradition Eleven (pointing to the anonymity pamphlet work) or on cable and 30-second public service announcements, citing budget, workload, recent Conference work on cable announcements, and the 15- and 30-second announcements already available.

themes.now: Tradition Eleven's short form ends "press, radio, and films"; the 2013 Conference affirmed that the internet and social media are implicit in that phrase. Any change to a Tradition needs the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups. The group and member estimates are now reference material kept by the office rather than part of the Final Report.
themes.now_cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 pp. 106, 124; p4137; 2026 Final Report p. 91
themes.asked: Seven proposals: a shorter, updated "Hope: Alcoholics Anonymous" video (#12); more guidance for A.A. social-media pages (#37); publishing group and membership estimates again (#74); adding "and the internet" to Tradition Eleven's short form (#116); adopting an Area 36 movie-theater public service announcement (#121); a national public information piece with QR codes (#140, Area 06); and one corrections pamphlet merging two pieces (#144).
raised: Item #12 asks for a shorter, current version of the Hope video; #121 points to a 30-second public service announcement that the Area 36 Public Information committee already shows in movie theaters in southern Minnesota.
Item #74 says the Final Report carried estimates continuously from 1951 through 2021 and suggests low-cost, estimate-based methods to resume them.

Item #37 asks for clearer guidance on keeping the Traditions on social-media pages that use the A.A. name at group, district and area level; #116 would name the internet in the short form of the Tradition itself.

Item #140 asks for one simple, consistent message usable across the U.S./Canada structure; #144 wants corrections volunteers to have guidance on qualifications and do's and don'ts like the treatment pamphlet "A.A. in Treatment Settings" (P-27) gives, plus background on the kinds of correctional facilities.

considerations.text: How a Tradition is changed: the Conference Charter requires the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups. In 1974 and 2013 the Conference chose to read the existing words as covering new media rather than change them.

On short videos, the 2026 Conference committee on Cooperation with the Professional Community recognized the need for short-form content and noted the office is already working in that direction; a development and review plan for public service announcements was accepted the same year.

Membership figures depend on group records: the office keeps no membership records, and its past estimates came from reports by listed groups. An A.A. World Services working group discussed improving the estimate material and data integrity, and the 2026 pilot survey tests ways to reach groups not registered with the office.
considerations.cite: 2022 Final Report p. 108; 2026 Final Report p. 17; p4276

considerations.text: Who reviews: the Conference Committee on Public Information reviews public information pamphlets, public service announcements, the membership survey and social media efforts; the Corrections committee recommends updates to corrections materials.

questions: How do newcomers in our area first hear about A.A. today: a video, social media, a friend, a professional?
Does Tradition Eleven's short form need new words, or does the 2013 reading that it already covers the internet serve us?
What would knowing A.A.'s estimated membership help us do, and how could numbers be gathered without burdening groups?
Should a video or public service announcement made by one area become a national piece, and what review should it go through first?
What guidance would our district's website or social media volunteers find most useful?
themes.watch: The trustees' Public Information Committee (Corrections for #144) decides this fall. Reports due to the 2027 Public Information committee cover public service announcements, new social-media accounts and the pilot membership survey.

themes.name: Grapevine and La Viña
themes.scope: The magazines and AA Grapevine, Inc.: print vs digital, price, subscription audit, La Viña books, story archive tags (Preamble items go to 'preamble').
themes.lede: AA Grapevine, Inc. publishes the monthly Grapevine and the bimonthly Spanish-language La Viña, as well as books, apps and a podcast. It has its own board and aims to pay its way through sales, without contributions. This year's five proposals cover print versus digital, price, a subscription audit, La Viña books and the online Story Archive.

background.text: Six volunteers founded Grapevine in June 1944. A.A. members serving in World War II called it their “meeting in print.” In 1986 the Conference recognized it as A.A.'s international journal, because individual issues cannot go through Conference approval.

Self-support through sales goes back decades. In 1989, with a price increase coming, delegates were asked to explain that Grapevine lives on subscription income and takes no group contributions. In 1994 all members were urged to help make the magazine self-supporting through subscriptions.

La Viña: in 1995 the Conference approved a bimonthly Spanish edition, with up to five years of funding from the Reserve Fund. The first issue appeared in June 1996. In 2001 the Conference kept La Viña as a Grapevine publication supported by the General Service Board as a service. In 2010 it set a goal of “spiritual parity” with Grapevine, starting with a 68-page bimonthly trial.
background.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 91; Advisory Actions p1660, p1665, p1677

background.text: In 2011 the Conference allowed Grapevine to sell magazines, books and products through apps, e-readers and online stores, provided its contracts protect the Traditions.

The Grapevine and La Viña apps launched in 2023. At its December 2023 strategic meeting, the Grapevine Board resolved to keep expanding digital delivery while continuing both print magazines. From April 15, 2024 the yearly Grapevine subscription rose to $36, the first increase in 12 years. The board cited the rising costs of paper, production and mailing.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report p. 21, p. 25; 2024 Final Report p. 19-20

background.text: In 2024 the Conference asked for a five-year financial plan for La Viña. In 2025 it called for both five-year plans to be reviewed every year, with at least five years of financial history, and for a member survey on the relevance, usefulness and financial viability of Grapevine's products.
background.cite: Advisory Actions p1712, p1713, p1715; 2025 Final Report p. 38

background.text: 2026: the Grapevine and La Viña committee accepted the Grapevine five-year plan. It took no action on a request that Grapevine accept contributions and extended the survey, with a progress report due at the 77th Conference (2027) and a final report at the 78th (2028). It also suggested that the Grapevine Board, with the General Service Board, explore more ways to support services that bring in no revenue. A Finance action rewrote the self-support pamphlet's question on Grapevine to list ways groups can support the magazines.

Last cycle, four proposals went to the AA Grapevine Board: contributions toward La Viña printing costs, larger type in Grapevine books, large-print Spanish titles, and the Preamble. None was forwarded to the Conference.

themes.now: Grapevine is partway through a multiyear turnaround: its loss fell from about $852,000 in 2024 to about $300,000 in 2025, and breakeven is expected in 2028. Most subscriptions are still print: 41,258 of 58,573 for Grapevine and 7,298 of 7,951 for La Viña. General Service Board support for La Viña was $480,315 in 2025, down from $755,749 in 2023.
themes.now_cite: 2026 Final Report p. 21-23, p. 25
themes.asked: Five proposals, all to the AA Grapevine Board: stop printing both magazines, keeping digital and print-at-home versions (#11). Raise Grapevine's price so all operations, podcast included, pay for themselves (#40). Tag Story Archive articles by or about the co-founders under related Steps and Tradition Four (#126). Audit five years of both magazines' subscriptions (#215). Plan for La Viña to roughly match Grapevine's book titles by 2029 (#216).
raised: The submitter of #11 proposes that both magazines continue online and in digital form, with a version members can download and print at home, in place of printed copies.
The submitter of #40 asks that the price take in every Grapevine cost so the whole operation is self-supporting. It names the magazine, digital and online subscriptions and the podcast.
The submitter of #216 points to the principle of “spiritual parity” and suggests drawing on La Viña material the Conference has already approved.

The submitter of #126 says added tags would let the archive's Step and Tradition filters find articles by or about Bill W. and Dr. Bob. The submitter of #215 asks for Grapevine and La Viña figures reported side by side, including delivery problems and customer-service complaints.

considerations.text: When the Grapevine Board decided to expand digital delivery, it said the print magazines would continue because they serve traditional subscribers, groups, newcomers and people in correctional facilities and other institutions. In 2025 the Carry the Message project filled 1,384 Grapevine and 197 La Viña subscriptions for members in need.
considerations.cite: 2024 Final Report p. 19-20; 2026 Final Report p. 22

considerations.text: Price and self-support: Grapevine does not accept contributions from groups or individuals, advertising or membership fees, and aims to live on sales. After the 2024 price increase, print subscription revenue rose 5% in 2025. The Grapevine Board's report linked some recent La Viña non-renewals to a price increase.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 79; 2026 Final Report p. 22, p. 25

considerations.text: Who decides: the AA Grapevine Board handles circulation, finance and publishing for both magazines. The Conference reviews Grapevine policies and the proposed topics for every Grapevine and La Viña book, but does not review magazine content before publication, and the Charter protects the editor's right to accept or reject material. Proposals on matters that belong to a board are sent to that board for its attention.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 78, p. 93, p. 137; 2026 Final Report p. 89

considerations.text: Related reporting: both five-year plans come back to the Conference every year with five years of financial history, and the 2025 committee followed up on La Viña subscription and fulfillment problems. The 2026 audit letter noted that Grapevine's revenue records rely on outside reports, with an upgraded platform from its fulfillment vendor expected in May 2026.
considerations.cite: Advisory Action p1713; 2025 Final Report p. 44; 2026 Final Report p. 24

questions: Does your group use the printed magazines, the apps, or both, and for what (meetings, newcomers, corrections, treatment)?
Should Grapevine's prices cover all of its costs, including services that bring in no revenue, or should some of those be supported another way?
What would “spiritual parity” between Grapevine and La Viña mean for Spanish-speaking members in your district?
What would you want a five-year subscription audit to show, and how would it fit with the yearly five-year-plan review and the member survey?
How do you search the Grapevine Story Archive now, and would Step and Tradition tags help?
themes.watch: After the fall board weekend (Oct 30 to Nov 2, 2026), watch the November preliminary agenda and the next status grid for any of these forwarded. At the April 2027 Conference, watch for the survey progress report and five-year-plan review.

themes.name: Conventions and forums
themes.scope: International Convention and Regional Forums: closing prayers, registration fees, an online special forum.
themes.lede: Proposals about A.A.'s big gatherings: the International Convention held every five years, and the Regional Forums, weekend sharing sessions where trustees and office staff meet members. They ask how Convention Big Meetings close, whether Forums should charge a fee, and about an online forum.

background.text: Regional Forums began in 1975 at the suggestion of the board's then-chair; in 1976 the Conference agreed to hold such regional gatherings as often as possible when a region asks, calling them Regional Forums.
In 1981 the Conference recommended that events such as the International Convention be self-supporting and never planned to run a deficit.

In 2015 the Conference added a Regional Forums section to the Service Manual describing their purpose, staffing, free registration and Forum reports. Regional Forums charge no registration fee and the board pays for meeting rooms; Local Forums are paid for locally.

After a late-2022 survey of the Fellowship, the trustees found no overwhelming desire to change the practice in which each Big Meeting chair chose to close with the Lord's Prayer, the Serenity Prayer or the Responsibility Statement; over half the responses favored it. The 2023 Conference committee agreed, and a floor motion to limit the options was sent back to the trustees.

In 2024 the Conference set six options for closing the Big Meetings: the Serenity Prayer, Responsibility Statement, Declaration of Unity, Third Step Prayer, Seventh Step Prayer or a moment of silence. The 2025 Convention in Vancouver used them.
background.cite: p2282; 2024 Final Report p. 38; 2026 Final Report p. 97

background.text: In 2025 and 2026 the trustees' committee took no action on proposals to return the Lord's Prayer: in 2025 it pointed to the 2024 Conference's thorough discussion, and in 2026 it called reconsidering the options premature.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report p. 99; 2026 Final Report p. 97

background.text: Online steps so far: Conference committees suggested virtual elements or a virtual forum (2023, 2024); a 2025 livestream pilot drew 433 remote attendees; a one-day online Special Forum for Deaf members on January 17, 2026 drew 389; staff are preparing a shorter online forum concept.
background.cite: 2023 Final Report p. 42; 2024 Final Report p. 45; 2026 Final Report p. 98

background.text: The four 2025 Regional Forums drew 2,004 people in person, 925 of them first-timers. Reviewing the 2026 budget, the trustees' committee noted that the cost per attendee has significantly increased and questioned the sustainability of in-person Forums.

themes.now: Since 2024 the Conference has provided six options for closing International Convention Big Meetings: the Serenity Prayer, Responsibility Statement, Declaration of Unity, Third Step Prayer, Seventh Step Prayer or silence. Regional Forums charge no registration fee; the General Service Board pays for meeting rooms.
themes.now_cite: p2282; Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 62
themes.asked: Three proposals are under review: adding the Lord's Prayer back beside the six current closing options for Convention Big Meetings (#198), a registration fee for Regional Forums (#190), and an online Special Forum for members of online groups outside the eight regions (#156, Area 51). A fourth (#154), a statement that the Lord's Prayer conflicts with the Preamble, is listed as withdrawn with no requested action.
raised: Item #198 says listing the Lord's Prayer again alongside the current options would give the meeting chair greater choice.

The withdrawn #154 argued the other way: that as a prayer of one faith it conflicts with the Preamble's statement that A.A. is not allied with any sect or denomination, and could be a barrier for some newcomers.
Item #156 (Area 51) would design the forum mainly for members of online groups that are not part of any of the eight regions; #190 gives no reason beyond the request.

considerations.text: The trustees' stated reasons for not reopening the closing options: the 2024 Conference discussed them thoroughly, the 2025 Convention put the six options into practice, and it is premature to reconsider.
considerations.cite: 2025 Final Report p. 99; 2026 Final Report p. 97

considerations.text: The no-fee rule is in the Service Manual's Regional Forums section, which the Conference added in 2015; the Conference Committee on Report and Charter reviews the manual and recommends changes.
Cost: the board pays for Regional Forum meeting rooms while Local Forums are paid for locally, and the trustees' committee has noted a significant rise in cost per attendee.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 62; 2026 Final Report p. 99

considerations.text: Special Forums already exist for members who would not normally be able to attend a Regional Forum or who have a need based on culture, language or geography, and one has been held online. The 2026 Conference committee suggested continuing to explore an abbreviated online forum.
considerations.cite: Service Manual 2026-2028 p. 62; 2026 Final Report pp. 47, 98

questions: What do the closing words of a large A.A. meeting mean to members of our group, and who should choose them?
Has anyone in our group attended a Regional Forum? Would a registration fee change whether they go?
Should A.A. hold an online forum, and who would it serve best?
How should the cost of Forums be shared between the Fellowship as a whole and the people who attend?
themes.watch: The trustees' International Conventions/Regional Forums Committee decides this fall. Watch the board's reports for the online forum concept and the paused livestream decision; bidding for the 2040 Convention opens in 2027.

themes.name: Safety and inclusion
themes.scope: Safety guidance, discrimination, which members literature serves or excludes (e.g. a pamphlet for transgender alcoholics), Double-Trouble groups in directories.
themes.lede: Proposals about safety in A.A. and about which members the literature speaks to: adding a statement on discrimination to A.A.'s safety service material, stopping work on the pamphlet being written for transgender alcoholics, and clarifying how 1986–87 guidance on “Double-Trouble” groups (groups with an outside affiliation) applies to the Meeting Guide app.

background.text: In 1986 the Conference decided that Double-Trouble groups would not be listed in A.A. directories. In 1987 it reaffirmed this, had existing listings removed, and defined such groups as groups with outside affiliation.

The pamphlet “A.A. and the Gay/Lesbian Alcoholic” was approved in 1989. In 2015 the Conference asked that it add the experience of bisexual, transgender and gender-nonconforming members, and the revision was approved in 2018 as “Experience, Strength and Hope: LGBTQ Alcoholics in A.A.”

In 2017 the Conference added text from the General Service Office (GSO) service piece “Safety and A.A.: Our Common Welfare” to the group pamphlet, “The A.A. Group” (P-16), added the word “safe” to one of its inventory questions, and asked the trustees to draft safety language for current and new recovery literature. In 2019 the Literature committee clarified that the safety language being drafted for Living Sober and the sponsorship pamphlet is meant to focus on safety at the group level.
background.cite: 2017 Final Report pp. 10-11 (p3030, p3032, p3039); 2019 Final Report p. 39

background.text: In 2019 a question and answer was added to “Understanding Anonymity”: speaking up about inappropriate behavior or calling the authorities does not go against the Traditions. In 2022 safety passages were added to “Questions and Answers on Sponsorship” (a sponsor stresses that A.A. should be a safe place for all members) and to chapter 29 of Living Sober (groups can keep a safe and secure environment by focusing on the common welfare and primary purpose).

In 2024 the Conference called for a pamphlet on the transgender alcoholic in A.A.; under the workload-sharing plan of those years the item was handled by the Conference Committee on Corrections. Progress reports came to the 2025 and 2026 Conferences; by 2026 there had been a call for stories, writing workshops and a working group.
background.cite: 2024 Final Report p. 38 (p1969); 2025 Final Report pp. 43-44; 2026 Final Report pp. 45, 102

background.text: In the 2025 cycle the trustees' Literature Committee did not forward a request for a pamphlet on inappropriate and sometimes illegal behavior in A.A., noting the importance of avoiding directive content and pointing to other sources of shared A.A. experience on safety.

In the 2025 and 2026 cycles the same committee did not forward requests to stop publishing pamphlets written for particular groups of alcoholics. In 2025 it said these pamphlets are meant to be inclusive and welcoming, not to exclude members or put up barriers; in 2026 it noted that each had been approved with substantial unanimity and that there was no widely expressed need to eliminate them.
background.cite: 2025 Final Report p. 108; 2026 Final Report pp. 104-105

background.text: Also in 2026, the Conference Committee on Treatment and Accessibilities chose not to adapt locally made safety videos, citing intellectual-property concerns and the substantial changes they would need, and instead asked A.A. World Services (AAWS) to create a new video from existing safety service material as budget permits.

themes.now: A.A.'s safety guidance includes General Service Office service material (“Safety and A.A.: Our Common Welfare” and the Safety Card for A.A. Groups) and safety passages added to Conference-approved literature since 2017. In 2026 the trustees said more safety publications are in development; a new safety video was requested. A transgender pamphlet draft or progress report is due in 2027.
themes.now_cite: 2017 Final Report pp. 10-11; 2018 Final Report p. 40; M-39 pp. 102, 104-105, 140; 2026 Final Report pp. 45, 53, 103, 105
themes.asked: Four items. Sent to A.A. World Services: 217, revising safety service material to say discrimination members experience is a safety issue (7, an April version, was superseded by 217), and 214, confirming the Double-Trouble directory guidance covers Meeting Guide. Sent to trustees' Literature: 100, stopping work on the transgender pamphlet. Related: 69 (Big Book stories), 68 (abuse, Step work).
